questions.question: A criminal deposits large amounts of cash from drug sales into several bank accounts in small sums. Which stage of money laundering does this illustrate?
options: Integration
Layering
Placement
Structuring of the economy
questions.explanation: Placement is the first stage, when criminal proceeds, often cash, are introduced into the financial system. Breaking deposits into small amounts to avoid attention is a common placement technique.
questions.reference: FATF; Central Bank AML/CFT Guidelines for the Financial Sector

questions.question: Moving funds through a series of transfers between accounts in different jurisdictions and different financial products to obscure their origin is known as:
options: layering
placement
integration
tipping off
questions.explanation: Layering involves complex layers of transactions designed to distance the funds from their criminal source and frustrate the audit trail.
questions.reference: FATF; Central Bank AML/CFT Guidelines for the Financial Sector

questions.question: A criminal uses funds that have already passed through several accounts to buy a property and a portfolio of investment funds, so that the money appears to be legitimate wealth. This is the:
options: placement stage
layering stage
reporting stage
integration stage
questions.explanation: Integration is the final stage, when laundered funds re-enter the legitimate economy, for example as investments or assets, appearing to be legitimate.
questions.reference: FATF; Central Bank AML/CFT Guidelines for the Financial Sector

questions.question: Under section 7 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, a person who handles the proceeds of criminal conduct commits a money laundering offence if they:
options: knew the property was the proceeds of criminal conduct, and only in that case
knew or believed, or were reckless as to whether, the property was the proceeds of criminal conduct
were convicted of the original crime that generated the proceeds
received a fee or commission for handling the property
questions.explanation: The mental element in section 7 is knowing or believing that the property is proceeds of criminal conduct, or being reckless as to whether it is. There is no requirement that the person committed the predicate offence or was paid.

questions.question: What is the maximum term of imprisonment on conviction on indictment for a money laundering offence under section 7 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010?
options: 5 years
10 years
14 years
Life imprisonment
questions.explanation: On conviction on indictment, section 7 provides for a fine, imprisonment for up to 14 years, or both. On summary conviction the maximum is a fine of up to €5,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment.

questions.question: A designated person fails to report a suspicious transaction as required by section 42 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010. On conviction on indictment the maximum penalty is:
options: a fine only, with no possibility of imprisonment
a fine and/or up to 14 years' imprisonment
a fine and/or up to 12 months' imprisonment
a fine and/or up to 5 years' imprisonment
questions.explanation: Failure to comply with section 42 is an offence punishable on indictment by a fine and/or up to 5 years' imprisonment (on summary conviction, up to €5,000 and/or 12 months). The 14-year maximum applies to the substantive money laundering offence.

questions.question: Which statement about the amendments to the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010 is correct?
options: The 2018 amending Act transposed the Fourth EU Money Laundering Directive and the 2021 amending Act transposed the Fifth
The 2018 amending Act transposed the Fifth Directive and the 2021 amending Act transposed the Sixth
The 2010 Act was repealed in 2021 and replaced by the EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation
The amending Acts only changed penalties and did not alter CDD requirements
questions.explanation: The Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) (Amendment) Act 2018 transposed 4AMLD, introducing for example the business risk assessment and domestic PEPs; the 2021 Amendment Act transposed 5AMLD. The 2010 Act remains in force, as amended, as of 2026.
questions.reference: CJA 2010 as amended by the 2018 and 2021 Amendment Acts

questions.question: Seán is a QFA working for a retail intermediary that advises on and arranges life assurance savings and investment policies. For the purposes of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, his firm is:
options: exempt, because only banks are covered
a designated person subject to the Act's obligations
covered only if it handles cash payments above €10,000
covered only for clients resident outside the EU
questions.explanation: Designated persons include credit and financial institutions, and financial institutions include insurance intermediaries acting in relation to life assurance and investment-related insurance. Such firms must apply CDD, report suspicions and maintain controls.

questions.question: Who is the competent authority for monitoring the AML/CFT compliance of credit and financial institutions in Ireland under the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010?
options: An Garda Síochána
The Revenue Commissioners
The Central Bank of Ireland
The Department of Finance
questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Ireland is the competent authority for credit and financial institutions. FIU Ireland (within An Garda Síochána) and Revenue receive suspicious transaction reports but do not supervise these firms' compliance.

questions.question: Under section 30A of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, a designated person's business risk assessment must:
options: be prepared by the Central Bank on the firm's behalf
only be prepared if the firm has had a suspicious transaction in the past year
be filed with FIU Ireland every quarter
be documented, approved by senior management, kept up to date and made available to the competent authority on request
questions.explanation: Section 30A requires the designated person to identify and assess its ML/TF risks, document the assessment (subject to a limited exception), have it approved by senior management, keep it up to date and make it available to its competent authority on request.

questions.question: Which set of factors must, at a minimum, be considered in a designated person's business risk assessment?
options: Customer types, products and services, countries or geographic areas, types of transactions, and delivery channels
Staff numbers, office locations, profitability and market share
Only the nationality of each customer
Only the size of each transaction
questions.explanation: Section 30A requires the assessment to cover the types of customers, products and services, countries or geographical areas, transactions and delivery channels, plus any prescribed factors, taking into account the national risk assessment and competent authority guidance.

questions.question: Under section 33 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, when must a designated person generally identify and verify a customer?
options: Only after the first annual review of the relationship
Before establishing a business relationship with the customer
Only if the customer pays in cash
Within 12 months after the business relationship starts
questions.explanation: CDD is required before establishing a business relationship, before carrying out an occasional transaction, where ML/TF is suspected, and where there are doubts about previously obtained identification information. Limited exceptions allow verification to be completed during the establishment of the relationship.

questions.question: For a designated person not covered by a special threshold, a single 'occasional transaction' (outside a business relationship) triggers CDD where the amount, or aggregate of linked amounts, is not less than:
questions.explanation: The general threshold in the definition of 'occasional transaction' is €15,000, whether in a single operation or linked operations. Lower thresholds apply to transfers of funds (€1,000) and certain other categories of designated person.

questions.question: Under the definition of 'occasional transaction' in the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, CDD for a transfer of funds is triggered where the amount to be transferred is in aggregate not less than:
questions.explanation: Transfers of funds have a lower threshold of €1,000. The €15,000 figure is the general threshold; €10,000 and €2,000 apply to specified other categories of designated person.

questions.question: A prospective client refuses to provide the identification documents a broker needs to complete customer due diligence. What does the Act require the broker to do?
options: Not provide the service or carry out the transaction, and discontinue any existing business relationship with the client
Proceed with the business but note the refusal on file
Proceed provided the client signs a declaration of identity
Proceed and complete CDD within the following 12 months
questions.explanation: Where a customer fails to provide the required documents or information, the designated person must not provide the service or carry out the transaction while the failure continues, and must discontinue the business relationship. It should also consider whether a suspicious transaction report is warranted.

questions.question: In what circumstances may a designated person complete verification of a customer's identity during, rather than before, the establishment of a business relationship?
options: Whenever the customer is a long-standing family friend of the adviser
Whenever the customer is resident in Ireland
Where verification beforehand would interrupt the normal conduct of business and there is no real risk of money laundering or terrorist financing, provided it is completed as soon as practicable
Never; verification must always be fully completed before any contact with the customer
questions.explanation: Section 33(5) allows verification to be completed during the establishment of the relationship if necessary not to interrupt the normal conduct of business and there is no real risk of ML/TF, but it must be completed as soon as practicable.

questions.question: When identifying the beneficial owner of a company customer, which ownership level is an indication of direct ownership under the EU AML framework applied in Ireland?
options: Any shareholding at all
A shareholding of 10% or more
A shareholding of 50% or more
A shareholding of 25% plus one share, or an ownership interest of more than 25%
questions.explanation: The Fourth AML Directive, applied through section 26 of the 2010 Act, treats a shareholding of 25% plus one share or an ownership interest of more than 25% as an indication of direct ownership, alongside control through other means.

questions.question: A firm has exhausted all possible means and cannot identify any natural person who owns or controls a corporate customer, and there are no grounds for suspicion. Who should be treated as the beneficial owner?
options: The company's external auditor
The natural person(s) holding the position of senior managing official
The company secretary's employer
No one; the firm may proceed without recording a beneficial owner
questions.explanation: Under the 4AMLD definition applied in Ireland, where no beneficial owner can be identified after exhausting all possible means and there are no grounds for suspicion, the senior managing official(s) are treated as beneficial owner, and the firm must keep records of the steps taken.

questions.question: In Ireland, the central register of beneficial ownership for companies is maintained by:
options: the Registrar of Beneficial Ownership (RBO)
the Central Bank of Ireland
FIU Ireland
the Data Protection Commission
questions.explanation: The Register of Beneficial Ownership of companies and industrial and provident societies is maintained by the Registrar of Beneficial Ownership. A separate register of beneficial ownership of trusts is maintained by the Revenue Commissioners. Designated persons should not rely solely on register information.

questions.question: Under the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010 as amended, a sitting member of Dáil Éireann who opens an investment account with an Irish firm is:
options: not a PEP, because only foreign office holders are PEPs
a PEP only if he or she is also a government minister
a politically exposed person, because domestic PEPs are covered
a PEP only if the investment exceeds €15,000
questions.explanation: Since the 2018 amendments, the PEP definition covers individuals entrusted with prominent public functions in Ireland as well as abroad, including members of parliament. There is no monetary threshold for PEP status.

questions.question: Which measures must a designated person apply when entering a business relationship with a PEP?
options: Refuse the business, because PEPs are prohibited customers
Apply simplified due diligence, because PEPs are publicly known
Notify FIU Ireland before accepting the business
Obtain senior management approval, determine the source of wealth and source of funds, and apply enhanced ongoing monitoring
questions.explanation: Section 37(4) requires senior management approval to establish or continue the relationship, measures to determine source of wealth and of funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring. PEP status is not itself a reason to refuse business or to file a report.

questions.question: Which of the following is a 'family member' of a PEP as defined in section 37 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010?
options: The PEP's parent
The PEP's cousin
The PEP's former school friend
The PEP's accountant
questions.explanation: Family members include a spouse or equivalent partner, children and their spouses or equivalent partners, and parents, plus any class the Minister prescribes. A business partner with joint beneficial ownership could be a 'close associate', but an accountant or friend is not automatically either.

questions.question: A former Government minister left office eight months ago and now wishes to invest with a broker. How should the broker treat her?
options: As an ordinary customer, because she no longer holds office
As a PEP, because the definition includes those entrusted with a prominent public function in the preceding 12 months, and PEP measures continue as long as the risk warrants
As a PEP for the rest of her life, with no possibility of reassessment
As a close associate rather than a PEP
questions.explanation: The section 37 definition includes individuals who are, or have been in the preceding 12 months, entrusted with a prominent public function. The Act also requires measures to continue for as long as reasonably required to address any continuing risk, so the 12 months is a minimum rather than an automatic cut-off.

questions.question: Under section 34A of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, a designated person may apply simplified customer due diligence where:
options: the customer is an Irish resident with a PPS number
the transaction is below €15,000

it has identified, in its business risk assessment, an area of lower risk into which the relationship falls and considers the relationship lower risk, recording its reasons and continuing sufficient monitoring
the customer has been referred by another regulated firm
questions.explanation: Simplified CDD is a risk-based judgement: the lower-risk area must be identified in the business risk assessment, the firm must record its reasons and evidence, and it must still monitor sufficiently to detect unusual or suspicious transactions.

questions.question: In which situation is enhanced customer due diligence required under the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010?
options: A customer established in a high-risk third country identified by the European Commission
A customer who is a salaried civil servant investing €5,000 from her own savings
A customer who is a publicly listed company on an EU regulated market
A customer who has been a client for over ten years
questions.explanation: Enhanced measures are required for customers established or residing in high-risk third countries identified by the Commission, for PEPs and their family members or close associates, and wherever the firm identifies higher risk.

questions.question: What does ongoing monitoring of a business relationship involve?
options: Re-identifying every customer from scratch each year, regardless of risk
Monitoring only the first transaction carried out by a new customer
Reviewing the customer's social media accounts weekly
Scrutinising transactions to ensure they are consistent with the firm's knowledge of the customer, its business and risk profile, and keeping CDD documents and information up to date
questions.explanation: Section 35(3) requires designated persons to monitor dealings with customers, including scrutinising transactions and source of funds, to the extent reasonably warranted by the risk, and to keep documents and information up to date.

questions.question: Gráinne, a QFA, has a long-standing client, a part-time retail worker, who suddenly wants to invest €400,000 in cash in a unit-linked bond and cannot explain where the money came from. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Accept the investment, because the client is long-standing and has passed CDD before
Tell the client she suspects money laundering and ask him to withdraw the application
Apply further scrutiny, seek to establish the source of funds, and report internally under the firm's procedures if suspicion remains
Accept the investment but ask the client to deposit it in instalments
questions.explanation: A transaction inconsistent with the customer's profile calls for further scrutiny of the source of funds. If knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds for suspicion arise, it must be reported under the firm's procedures and onward to FIU Ireland and Revenue. Telling the client of the suspicion risks tipping off, and splitting the deposit would facilitate structuring.

questions.question: To whom must a designated person in Ireland submit a suspicious transaction report under section 42 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010?
options: The Central Bank of Ireland only
FIU Ireland (An Garda Síochána) and the Revenue Commissioners
The Data Protection Commission
The customer's bank
questions.explanation: Section 42 requires reports to be made to FIU Ireland and to the Revenue Commissioners. The Central Bank is the supervisor but is not the recipient of STRs.

questions.question: The reporting obligation in section 42 is triggered where a designated person:
options: has proof beyond reasonable doubt that money laundering has occurred
has been told by An Garda Síochána that a customer is under investigation
has been asked by the customer to keep a transaction confidential
knows, suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect that another person has been or is engaged in money laundering or terrorist financing
questions.explanation: The test includes an objective element: 'reasonable grounds to suspect'. A designated person cannot avoid the obligation by ignoring obvious warning signs, and proof is not required.

questions.question: Under section 42 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, which statement about timing is correct?
options: The report must be made as soon as practicable, and the designated person should generally not proceed with the suspicious transaction before reporting unless that is impracticable or likely to alert the customer
The report must be made within 30 days, and the transaction must always be completed first
The report must be made only once the transaction has been completed, to avoid tipping off
The report must be made within 72 hours, and the transaction must be cancelled in every case
questions.explanation: Section 42(2) requires the report as soon as practicable after the knowledge or suspicion arises. Section 42(7) generally prohibits proceeding with the suspicious transaction or service before reporting, with exceptions where delay is not practicable or could alert the customer.

questions.question: After his firm submits a suspicious transaction report, Dara, an adviser, phones the client and says: 'You might want to be careful, our compliance team has reported your account.' Dara has most likely committed:
options: no offence, because the report had already been sent
a breach of the GDPR only
the offence of tipping off
the offence of failing to report
questions.explanation: Section 49 makes it an offence to disclose information likely to prejudice an investigation arising from a report, or a contemplated or ongoing investigation. The penalty on indictment is a fine and/or up to 5 years' imprisonment.

questions.question: For how long must a designated person keep CDD documents and records of a business relationship after the relationship ends (or the last transaction, if later)?
options: At least 5 years
At least 1 year
At least 3 years
Indefinitely
questions.explanation: Section 55 requires records to be retained for not less than 5 years after the relevant date, such as the end of the service to the customer or the last transaction. Personal data held solely for this purpose must then be deleted unless an extension applies.

questions.question: Under the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, who may direct a designated person to retain AML records beyond the standard retention period, and for how long?
options: The customer, for any period they choose
The Data Protection Commission, for up to 2 further years
The firm's external auditor, for up to 10 further years
A member of An Garda Síochána not below the rank of sergeant, for up to a further 5 years, where needed for an ML/TF investigation or prosecution
questions.explanation: Section 55(4A) to (4C) allows a Garda of at least sergeant rank to direct in writing that records be kept for up to a further 5 years where necessary for an investigation or likely prosecution, after assessing necessity and proportionality.

questions.question: Section 54 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010 requires a designated person to:
options: outsource all AML compliance to an external firm
adopt internal policies, controls and procedures to prevent and detect ML/TF, and ensure relevant staff are instructed in the law and trained to identify suspicious transactions
train only the compliance officer, as other staff do not need AML training
publish its AML policies on its website
questions.explanation: Section 54 requires documented policies and procedures (covering areas such as risk assessment, CDD, monitoring, reporting and record keeping) and ongoing training for persons involved in the business, including in identifying suspicious activity.

questions.question: A broker relies on another regulated financial institution to carry out CDD on a shared client, as permitted under section 40 of the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010. If the CDD proves inadequate, who remains responsible for the broker's compliance?
options: The other institution only
The Central Bank, as it authorised both firms
The broker, which remains responsible for compliance with its CDD obligations
Nobody, because reliance transfers all liability
questions.explanation: Reliance on a relevant third party is permitted in specified circumstances, but the designated person remains liable for any failure to apply the required measures.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes terrorist financing from money laundering?
options: Terrorist financing only involves cash, whereas money laundering only involves electronic transfers
Terrorist financing can involve funds from legitimate sources, because the focus is on the intended use of the funds
Terrorist financing is not covered by Irish AML legislation
Terrorist financing only occurs where the amount exceeds €15,000
questions.explanation: Money laundering concerns disguising the criminal origin of proceeds, whereas terrorist financing concerns providing or collecting funds intending or knowing they will be used for terrorism, so the funds may be legitimately earned. The 2010 Act applies its preventive obligations to both.
questions.reference: Criminal Justice (Terrorist Offences) Act 2005, s.13; CJA 2010

questions.question: During onboarding, a firm finds that a prospective client is a person designated under EU financial sanctions. What is the correct response?
options: Proceed, as EU sanctions only bind banks
Proceed, but apply enhanced due diligence
Ask the client whether the listing is accurate and proceed if he says it is not
Not make funds or economic resources available, freeze any funds held, and report to the Central Bank of Ireland as the competent authority for financial sanctions
questions.explanation: EU sanctions regulations apply directly to all persons in the EU. Firms must freeze funds of designated persons, must not make funds available to them, and must report to the competent authority, which in Ireland for financial sanctions is the Central Bank.
questions.reference: EU sanctions regulations; Central Bank of Ireland financial sanctions guidance

questions.question: What is the Financial Action Task Force (FATF)?
options: An inter-governmental body that sets international standards (the FATF Recommendations) for combating money laundering and terrorist financing
The Irish police unit that receives suspicious transaction reports
An EU agency that directly supervises Irish banks
A trade body representing financial advisers in Europe
questions.explanation: FATF is an inter-governmental policy-making body whose Recommendations form the global AML/CFT standard; it also evaluates countries' compliance through mutual evaluations. FIU Ireland, not FATF, receives Irish STRs.

questions.question: As of November 2026, which statement about the EU AML package is accurate?
options: The EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation has applied directly in Ireland since January 2025 and fully replaced the 2010 Act
The Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) is based in Dublin and supervises all Irish retail intermediaries
The AML Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 is due to apply from 10 July 2027, and AMLA, based in Frankfurt, is due to begin direct supervision of selected high-risk entities from 2028
The EU AML package was withdrawn and will not take effect
questions.explanation: As of 2026 the AMLR is scheduled to apply from 10 July 2027, while AMLA, established in Frankfurt, will directly supervise a limited number of selected cross-border financial entities from 2028. Until then, the 2010 Act as amended remains the Irish framework, with the Central Bank as supervisor.

questions.question: Which body authorises, registers or licenses most financial service providers operating in Ireland?
options: The Department of Finance
The Central Bank of Ireland
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
questions.explanation: The Central Bank of Ireland is the authority that authorises, registers or licenses financial service providers in Ireland (banking licences are granted by the ECB on the Central Bank's proposal under the SSM). The FSPO and CCPC have no authorisation role.

questions.question: Under the Single Supervisory Mechanism, the decision to grant a banking licence to a new credit institution established in Ireland is taken by:
options: the Central Bank of Ireland alone
the Minister for Finance
the European Central Bank, on a proposal from the Central Bank of Ireland
the European Banking Authority
questions.explanation: Under the SSM, the ECB grants and withdraws licences for all euro-area credit institutions. The application is made to the national authority (the Central Bank), which assesses it and proposes a decision to the ECB.
questions.reference: SSM Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013, Art. 14; Central Bank Act 1971, s.9

questions.question: Insurance and reinsurance undertakings in Ireland are authorised under:
options: the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
the Consumer Credit Act 1995
the European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018
the European Union (Insurance and Reinsurance) Regulations 2015 (Solvency II)
questions.explanation: Insurers (the product producers) are authorised under the Solvency II Regulations 2015. The IDD Regulations 2018 govern insurance distribution, including the registration of insurance intermediaries.
questions.reference: European Union (Insurance and Reinsurance) Regulations 2015 (S.I. No. 485 of 2015)

questions.question: A firm wishing to provide investment services in financial instruments within the scope of MiFID II, such as portfolio management, must be authorised under:
options: the European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017
the Central Bank Act 1997, Part V
the European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018
the Credit Union Act 1997
questions.explanation: MiFID II was transposed in Ireland by the European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017, under which investment firms are authorised by the Central Bank.
questions.reference: European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017 (S.I. No. 375 of 2017)

questions.question: A retail intermediary gives advice on, and receives and transmits orders in, collective investment schemes. It does not hold client money and qualifies for the MiFID II Article 3 exemption. Under which legislation is it typically authorised?
options: The Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
The European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017, with a full MiFID passport
The Credit Union Act 1997
No authorisation is needed for MiFID-exempt firms
questions.explanation: Firms exempt from MiFID under Article 3 can be authorised under the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995 as investment business firms. Exemption from MiFID does not mean exemption from authorisation.
questions.reference: Investment Intermediaries Act 1995; MiFID II Art. 3

questions.question: An insurance intermediary must be registered with the Central Bank under:
options: the Consumer Credit Act 1995
the European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018
the Investor Compensation Act 1998
the Pensions Act 1990
questions.explanation: The Insurance Distribution Directive was transposed by the European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018, which require insurance and reinsurance intermediaries to be registered with the Central Bank.
questions.reference: European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 229 of 2018)

questions.question: A firm that wishes to arrange mortgages for consumers on behalf of lenders needs authorisation as a mortgage intermediary under:
options: the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995 only
the European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018
the Consumer Credit Act 1995 and the European Union (Consumer Mortgage Credit Agreements) Regulations 2016
the Central Bank Act 1971
questions.explanation: Mortgage intermediaries are authorised under the Consumer Credit Act 1995; the Consumer Mortgage Credit Agreements Regulations 2016 (transposing the Mortgage Credit Directive) add requirements for mortgage credit intermediaries.
questions.reference: Consumer Credit Act 1995, s.116; S.I. No. 142 of 2016

questions.question: A non-bank lender providing personal loans to consumers in Ireland would usually need authorisation as a:
options: credit union under the Credit Union Act 1997
payment institution
credit servicing firm only
retail credit firm under Part V of the Central Bank Act 1997
questions.explanation: Non-bank lenders that provide credit directly to individuals are authorised as retail credit firms under Part V of the Central Bank Act 1997 (as amended). Credit servicing firms manage loans but are a separate category.

questions.question: The Consumer Protection (Regulation of Retail Credit and Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2022 brought which providers within the Central Bank's authorisation regime?
options: Providers of hire-purchase, consumer-hire and buy now pay later (BNPL) agreements
Credit unions
Pension scheme trustees
Insurance brokers
questions.explanation: The 2022 Act extended the definition of retail credit (and credit servicing) to cover hire-purchase, consumer-hire and BNPL providers, so these firms need Central Bank authorisation.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection (Regulation of Retail Credit and Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2022

questions.question: The main purpose of requiring credit servicing firms to be authorised by the Central Bank was to:
options: allow credit servicing firms to take deposits
ensure borrowers whose loans were sold to unregulated entities kept the protections they had with the original regulated lender
allow credit unions to sell their loan books
exempt loan purchasers from the Consumer Protection Code
questions.explanation: The Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2015 required firms managing loans sold by regulated lenders to be authorised, so borrowers keep protections such as the CPC and the Code of Conduct on Mortgage Arrears (now incorporated into the revised CPC).
questions.reference: Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2015

questions.question: The Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2018 extended the regime so that authorisation is also required by:
options: every borrower who refinances a loan
debt collection agencies acting for utility companies
entities that hold the legal title to the loans (the loan owners), not only the firms that service them
credit reference agencies
questions.explanation: The 2018 Act extended credit servicing to include holding the legal title to credit, so 'vulture fund' loan owners must themselves be authorised (or hold title through an authorised entity), not just their servicers.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection (Regulation of Credit Servicing Firms) Act 2018

questions.question: A firm providing money remittance or payment initiation services (and not a bank) is authorised as a payment institution under:
options: the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
the Consumer Credit Act 1995
the European Union (Electronic Money) Regulations 2011
the European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018
questions.explanation: Payment institutions are authorised under the Payment Services Regulations 2018, which transposed PSD2. Electronic money institutions are authorised under the separate E-Money Regulations 2011.
questions.reference: European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 6 of 2018)

questions.question: A firm that issues electronic money (e-money) and is not a credit institution must be authorised as:
options: an electronic money institution under the European Union (Electronic Money) Regulations 2011
a retail credit firm
a mortgage intermediary
an investment business firm under the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
questions.explanation: E-money issuers (other than banks) are authorised as electronic money institutions under the European Union (Electronic Money) Regulations 2011, which transposed the E-Money Directive.
questions.reference: European Union (Electronic Money) Regulations 2011 (S.I. No. 183 of 2011)

questions.question: Credit unions in Ireland are registered and regulated under:
options: the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
the Credit Union Act 1997, with the Registry of Credit Unions in the Central Bank responsible for their regulation
the Consumer Credit Act 1995 only
the European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017
questions.explanation: Credit unions are registered under the Credit Union Act 1997 (as amended). The Registrar of Credit Unions, within the Central Bank, is responsible for their regulation and supervision.

questions.question: A high cost credit provider (formerly called a moneylender) must hold:
options: a banking licence granted by the ECB
a registration under the IDD Regulations 2018
a licence from the Central Bank under the Consumer Credit Act 1995, renewed annually
no licence, provided the APR is disclosed to customers
questions.explanation: High cost credit providers are licensed by the Central Bank under the Consumer Credit Act 1995. A licence lasts for 12 months, so the provider must apply to renew it each year.
questions.reference: Consumer Credit Act 1995 (as amended), Part VIII

questions.question: Under MiFID II, a tied agent:
options: can act for several investment firms at once to obtain the best deal for clients
must hold its own MiFID authorisation and passport
may hold client money in its own name
acts on behalf of only one investment firm, which takes full and unconditional responsibility for the agent's actions
questions.explanation: A MiFID tied agent acts under the full and unconditional responsibility of a single investment firm. It does not need its own authorisation but must be entered in a public register.
questions.reference: MiFID II, Art. 29; S.I. No. 375 of 2017

questions.question: When an investment firm appoints a tied agent under MiFID II, the tied agent must be:
options: entered in a public register
authorised by ESMA
approved by the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
a member of the Deposit Guarantee Scheme
questions.explanation: MiFID II requires tied agents to be entered in a public register in the Member State where they are established, so clients can check their status.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), an intermediary may describe itself to consumers as a 'broker' only if:
options: it holds appointments from at least three product producers
its principal regulated activities are provided on the basis of a fair analysis of the market
it charges a fee instead of receiving commission
it has been authorised for at least five years
questions.explanation: The term 'broker' requires the intermediary's principal regulated activities to be provided on the basis of a fair analysis of the market. There is no fixed number of appointments and no ban on commission for using 'broker'.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), an intermediary that is tied to a single product producer for a particular financial service must:
options: refuse to deal with consumers who want a comparison
describe itself as 'independent'
disclose that fact to the consumer in all communications relating to that service
obtain the Central Bank's approval for each sale
questions.explanation: A tied intermediary must disclose its tied status in all communications with the consumer about the relevant service. A tied intermediary cannot claim to be 'independent'.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), an intermediary that does NOT provide a service on the basis of a fair analysis of the market must:
options: stop providing that service
describe itself as a broker
refer the consumer to the FSPO
clearly disclose to the consumer the names of the product producers whose products it will consider
questions.explanation: Where there is no fair analysis of the market, the intermediary must clearly disclose the names of the product producers it intends to consider, so the consumer understands how limited the search is.

questions.question: An Irish-authorised firm sells to customers in Spain directly from Ireland without setting up any office in Spain. This is an example of:
options: freedom to provide services
freedom of establishment
a third-country branch
a tied agency arrangement
questions.explanation: Providing services cross-border without a physical presence in the host state uses the freedom to provide services. Setting up a branch in the host state uses the freedom of establishment.
questions.reference: EU passporting - Treaty freedoms; MiFID II / IDD passporting provisions

questions.question: An Irish-authorised insurance intermediary wants to open a branch in Germany. How does it exercise its passport?
options: It applies directly to the German regulator for a full new authorisation
It notifies the Central Bank of Ireland (its home regulator), which passes the information to the German authority
It needs approval from EIOPA
No notification is needed because both states are in the EU
questions.explanation: Passporting is done through the home state regulator: the firm notifies the Central Bank, which forwards the notification to the host state authority. No new authorisation is needed, but a notification is always required.
questions.reference: IDD passporting notification procedures; European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018

questions.question: A retail intermediary authorised only under the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995, relying on the MiFID II Article 3 exemption, wishes to advise clients in France. Which statement is correct?
options: It may passport into France on a freedom of services basis by notifying the Central Bank
It may passport into France only by opening a branch
It does not benefit from a MiFID passport, because the Article 3 exemption gives no passporting rights
It may passport into France if it appoints a tied agent there
questions.explanation: Firms exempt from MiFID II under Article 3 are regulated nationally and do not get the MiFID passport. To passport investment services they would need full MiFID authorisation.
questions.reference: MiFID II, Art. 3; Investment Intermediaries Act 1995

questions.question: A life assurer authorised in another EEA state sells policies to Irish consumers through a branch in Dublin. Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025):
options: the Code does not apply, because the insurer is supervised by its home state
the Code applies only if the consumer is a company
the Code applies only to advertising
the Code applies, because 'regulated entity' includes firms authorised in other EEA states that provide regulated activities in the State
questions.explanation: The CPC's definition of regulated entity covers firms authorised by the Central Bank and firms authorised in another EU/EEA state when providing regulated activities in Ireland. Prudential supervision stays with the home state, but Irish conduct rules apply.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 2 (definition of regulated entity)

questions.question: Before dealing with a financial firm, a consumer wants to confirm that it is authorised. The best place to check is:
options: the Central Bank of Ireland's public registers
the firm's own advertising
the Companies Registration Office only
the FSPO's published decisions
questions.explanation: The Central Bank publishes registers of authorised, registered and licensed firms (registers.centralbank.ie). Being registered as a company with the CRO does not mean a firm is authorised to provide financial services.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), a mortgage lender must:
options: appoint at least ten mortgage intermediaries
maintain a public register of the mortgage intermediaries it has appointed
ensure all mortgage intermediaries are tied to it
register its appointed intermediaries with the FSPO
questions.explanation: Lenders must maintain a register of the mortgage intermediaries they have appointed and make it available to the public, so consumers can check an intermediary's appointment.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), a firm authorised by the Central Bank must include a regulatory disclosure statement on its stationery and website, in a prescribed form. Which is the correct approach?
options: '[Firm name] is approved and guaranteed by the Central Bank of Ireland'
Any wording the firm chooses, provided the Central Bank is mentioned
'[Firm name, trading as ...] is regulated by the Central Bank of Ireland', presented so that it does not look like an endorsement by the Central Bank
No statement is needed if the firm is listed on the Central Bank register
questions.explanation: The statement must follow the prescribed format and must not be presented so as to appear to be an endorsement by the Central Bank. Firms authorised in another Member State use a different prescribed format naming their home regulator.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of requiring intermediaries to hold professional indemnity insurance (PII)?
options: To guarantee the investment returns of clients
To cover the intermediary's office property against fire and theft
To replace the need for a complaints procedure
To ensure funds are available to meet claims arising from professional negligence, such as unsuitable advice
questions.explanation: PII protects clients (and the firm) by ensuring the intermediary can meet liability claims arising from negligence in its professional activities. It does not guarantee investment performance.
questions.reference: IDD Art. 10(4); Mortgage Credit Directive Art. 29

questions.question: Under the Insurance Distribution Directive, as transposed in Ireland, an insurance intermediary's professional indemnity insurance must:
options: cover the whole territory of the European Union
cover only claims made by Irish residents
be provided by the Central Bank
be held only by intermediaries that charge fees
questions.explanation: The IDD requires PII (or a comparable guarantee) covering the whole territory of the Union, at least at the minimum amounts set under the Directive (unless the insurer has already taken full responsibility for the intermediary).
questions.reference: IDD Art. 10(4); European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018

questions.question: A company advertises investment services to Irish consumers without being authorised by the Central Bank or any other EEA regulator. Which statement is correct?
options: This is permitted as long as the company is registered with the Companies Registration Office
Providing regulated financial services without authorisation is an offence, and the Central Bank publishes warnings naming unauthorised firms
The only consequence is that the company cannot advertise on television
The company only needs authorisation once it has 100 clients
questions.explanation: Carrying on regulated business without authorisation is a criminal offence under the relevant legislation (e.g. the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995, the Central Bank Act 1971). The Central Bank publishes an unauthorised firms warning list to alert consumers.
questions.reference: Investment Intermediaries Act 1995; Central Bank unauthorised firms warnings

questions.question: Why is it risky for a consumer to invest through a firm that is not authorised?
options: Unauthorised firms always charge higher fees
Investments arranged by unauthorised firms are always illegal for the consumer to hold
The consumer would generally not benefit from regulatory protections such as the Consumer Protection Code and the Investor Compensation Scheme
The consumer would have to pay income tax twice
questions.explanation: Protections such as the CPC, the Fitness and Probity regime and the Investor Compensation Scheme apply to authorised firms. A consumer using an unauthorised firm generally loses these safeguards.
questions.reference: Central Bank Consumer Hub; Investor Compensation Act 1998

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical ground on which the Central Bank may revoke a firm's authorisation?
options: The firm's profits fell in the last financial year
The firm changed its trading name
The firm opened a second office in Ireland
The firm no longer meets the conditions of its authorisation, or has seriously breached regulatory requirements
questions.explanation: Authorisations can be revoked where the firm no longer meets the conditions of authorisation (e.g. fitness and probity, capital, PII) or has committed serious breaches, as well as at the firm's own request.
questions.reference: Investment Intermediaries Act 1995; CRD Art. 18; IDD Regulations 2018

questions.question: Under the Capital Requirements Directive, a credit institution's authorisation may be withdrawn if it:
options: does not make use of the authorisation within 12 months, or has ceased business for more than 6 months
makes a loss in any single quarter
refuses to open a branch in every Member State
fails to advertise its products for six months
questions.explanation: Among the grounds in CRD Article 18 are failure to use the authorisation within 12 months, express renunciation, or ceasing business for more than six months, as well as ceasing to meet the conditions of authorisation.

questions.question: Siobhan has just obtained her QFA and wants to set up her own business advising consumers on pensions and life assurance. Which statement is correct?
options: Her QFA qualification is itself an authorisation to trade
Her business must still be authorised or registered by the Central Bank (e.g. registered as an insurance intermediary); the QFA meets the individual competency requirement
She needs only to register with the Pensions Authority
She can trade without authorisation for the first two years
questions.explanation: Qualifications demonstrate individual competence under the Minimum Competency Code; they are not an authorisation. The firm must be authorised or registered under the relevant legislation, and its PCF holders must be approved.

questions.question: Declan plans a new firm that will advise consumers on life assurance and pension policies, arrange household insurance, and arrange mortgages on behalf of several lenders. Which combination of authorisations does the firm need?
options: A banking licence only
MiFID authorisation only, as this covers all retail advice

Registration as an insurance intermediary under the IDD Regulations 2018, and authorisation as a mortgage intermediary under the Consumer Credit Act 1995 (and the Consumer Mortgage Credit Agreements Regulations 2016)
No authorisation, as long as each staff member holds the QFA
questions.explanation: Insurance products (including life assurance and insurance-based pension policies) are covered by IDD registration, while arranging mortgages needs mortgage intermediary authorisation. Advising on non-insurance investments would additionally require IIA 1995 or MiFID authorisation.
questions.reference: IDD Regulations 2018; Consumer Credit Act 1995, s.116; S.I. No. 142 of 2016

questions.question: When a new firm applies for authorisation, the people proposed for pre-approval controlled functions (e.g. directors) must:
options: be shareholders in the firm
be resident in Ireland for at least five years
simply be named in the application, with no assessment
be approved by the Central Bank under the Fitness and Probity regime before taking up their roles
questions.explanation: The Central Bank assesses the fitness and probity of proposed PCF holders (usually through an online questionnaire and, where needed, interview) and must approve them before they take up their roles.

questions.question: Before a PRSA product can be offered to the public, the product must be approved by:
options: the Pensions Authority and Revenue
the FSPO and the CCPC
EIOPA
the Department of Social Protection
questions.explanation: PRSA products are approved by both the Pensions Authority (product approval under the Pensions Act 1990) and Revenue (tax approval). PRSA providers themselves must be authorised financial institutions.

questions.question: From what date did the revised Consumer Protection Code replace the Consumer Protection Code 2012?
options: 1 January 2025
24 March 2025
24 March 2026
1 January 2027
questions.explanation: The revised Code was published on 24 March 2025 and applied from 24 March 2026, giving firms a 12-month implementation period. CPC 2012 applied until then.

questions.question: The revised Consumer Protection Code is made up mainly of which two statutory instruments?
options: The Minimum Competency Regulations 2017 and the Fitness and Probity Standards
The Investment Intermediaries Act 1995 and the Consumer Credit Act 1995
The IDD Regulations 2018 and the MiFID Regulations 2017
The Standards for Business Regulations 2025 (s.17A, Central Bank Reform Act 2010) and the Consumer Protection Regulations 2025 (s.48, Central Bank (Supervision and Enforcement) Act 2013)
questions.explanation: The revised Code comprises the Standards for Business Regulations (S.I. No. 80 of 2025) and the Consumer Protection Regulations (S.I. No. 81 of 2025), supported by Central Bank guidance.

questions.question: Under the General Principles of the Consumer Protection Code 2012, a regulated entity must act:
options: honestly, fairly and professionally in the best interests of its customers and the integrity of the market
in the best interests of its shareholders before those of its customers
only in accordance with the written terms of each contract
in whatever way maximises sales of its own products
questions.explanation: The first General Principle of CPC 2012 required firms to act honestly, fairly and professionally in the best interests of customers and the integrity of the market. Under the revised Code, this approach continues through the Standards for Business (e.g. securing customers' interests).

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code 2012, an incorporated body is a 'consumer' if its annual turnover in the previous financial year did not exceed:
options: €1 million
€3 million
€5 million
€10 million
questions.explanation: CPC 2012 included incorporated bodies with turnover of €3 million or less (not part of a group with combined turnover above €3 million). The revised Code raised this threshold to €5 million.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), a company is a 'consumer' if its annual turnover in the previous financial year (and that of any group it belongs to) did not exceed:
options: €3 million
€10 million
€2 million
€5 million
questions.explanation: The revised Code raised the turnover threshold from €3 million (CPC 2012) to €5 million, bringing more small businesses within its protections. Natural persons and groups such as partnerships, clubs and charities are also consumers.

questions.question: In the Consumer Protection Code, a 'personal consumer' is:
options: a natural person acting outside his or her business, trade or profession
any customer with an annual income below €50,000
any sole trader
a company with fewer than ten employees
questions.explanation: A personal consumer is a natural person acting outside their business, trade or profession. Many rules, e.g. on affordability and personal loans, apply specifically to personal consumers.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 2(1); CPC 2012 Definitions

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), a 'consumer in vulnerable circumstances' is a natural person whose personal circumstances:
options: mean they are over 70 years of age
mean they have a medical card
whether permanent or temporary, make them especially susceptible to harm, particularly where the firm is not acting with appropriate care
mean they have been refused credit in the past
questions.explanation: The revised Code uses a broad, circumstances-based definition recognising that anyone can move in and out of vulnerability (e.g. bereavement, illness, job loss). It is not based on age or any single characteristic.

questions.question: How did the Consumer Protection Code 2012 define a 'vulnerable consumer'?
options: Any consumer aged over 65
A consumer who has made a complaint to the FSPO
Any consumer in mortgage arrears
A natural person who has capacity to make their own decisions but, because of individual circumstances, may need assistance to do so; or who has limited capacity to make their own decisions
questions.explanation: CPC 2012 focused on a person's capacity and need for assistance in making decisions. The revised Code replaced this with the broader 'consumer in vulnerable circumstances' concept.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), what is the status of a 'trusted contact person' nominated by a personal consumer?
options: The firm may contact them in specified circumstances, but they have no authority to deal with the consumer's affairs
They automatically hold power of attorney over the consumer's accounts
They must be a family member of the consumer
The firm must appoint one for every customer aged over 70
questions.explanation: At a personal consumer's request, a firm records a trusted contact person, with written consent from both. The trusted contact has no authority to transact on or deal with the consumer's affairs.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), how often must a firm review whether its arrangements for training staff on consumers in vulnerable circumstances are adequate, and report to its board?
options: Every 5 years
At least once every 2 years
Every 6 months
Only when the Central Bank requests it
questions.explanation: The firm must review at least once every 2 years whether the vulnerability training requirements are being met, and report to the board. Training must reach relevant staff, not just customer-facing teams.

questions.question: A consumer refuses to provide information a firm needs to assess suitability for an investment. Under the Consumer Protection Code, the firm should:
options: proceed and assume the consumer is a cautious investor
proceed and record that the consumer was uncooperative
inform the consumer that it cannot provide the service without that information
refer the consumer to the FSPO
questions.explanation: A firm cannot assess suitability without adequate information. Where the consumer will not provide it, the firm must tell them it cannot offer the service. This rule exists under both CPC 2012 and the revised Code.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 16(11); CPC 2012, Chapter 5

questions.question: Aoife, a QFA, recommends a pension to a client. Under the Consumer Protection Code, what must she do with the statement of suitability?
options: Prepare, sign and date it, and give it to the client before the product is provided, setting out why the recommendation is suitable
Prepare it only if the client asks for it
Send it to the Central Bank within 5 working days
Give it to the client within 30 days after the policy starts
questions.explanation: The firm must prepare a written statement of suitability, signed and dated, explaining why the product is considered suitable, and give it to the consumer before providing the service. The revised Code also requires a prescribed 'Important Notice' at the start.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 18; CPC 2012, Chapter 5

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), the suitability exemption for a consumer who chooses a product without assistance from the firm does NOT apply where the personal consumer is seeking:
options: a car insurance policy
a current account
a mortgage loan, a home reversion agreement or credit above €75,000
a term deposit of less than one year
questions.explanation: Even where the consumer selects the product themselves, a personal consumer seeking credit above €75,000, a mortgage or a home reversion agreement must still have suitability assessed. For investment products chosen without assistance, a warning on paper or durable medium is required.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, unless otherwise agreed with the consumer, unsolicited personal visits or telephone contact may take place only:
options: between 8am and 8pm, Monday to Friday
between 9am and 9pm, Monday to Saturday, excluding public holidays
between 9am and 6pm, any day
between 10am and 10pm, Monday to Sunday
questions.explanation: Both CPC 2012 and the revised Code restrict unsolicited contact to 9am-9pm, Monday to Saturday, excluding public holidays, unless otherwise agreed with the consumer.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 112; CPC 2012, Chapter 3

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), an unsolicited personal visit to a consumer who is a natural person is permitted only where:
options: the firm has visited the consumer before
the visit is during business hours
the consumer is an existing customer
the consumer has given written consent in advance for that visit, covering its purpose, time, date and location and any fee
questions.explanation: The revised Code prohibits unsolicited personal visits to natural persons unless the consumer gives prior written consent for each visit, including details of purpose, timing, location and fees.

questions.question: When making an unsolicited contact, what must a firm's representative do immediately?
options: Ask for the consumer's PPS number
Read out the firm's full terms of business
Identify themselves and the firm they represent, and explain the purpose of the contact
Ask the consumer to confirm their annual income
questions.explanation: The representative must immediately give their name, the regulated entity's name and the purpose of the contact, disclose any call recording, and end the contact if the consumer does not want to proceed.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 113; CPC 2012, Chapter 3

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, when must an intermediary first provide its terms of business to a consumer?
options: Only if the consumer makes a complaint
Within 10 working days after the first sale
Only when the consumer signs a contract
Before providing the first service to that consumer
questions.explanation: Terms of business must be drawn up and given to the consumer before the first service is provided. Under the revised Code they must also be a stand-alone document and be published on the firm's website.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 51; CPC 2012, Chapter 4

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, prescribed warning statements in documents and advertisements must be:
options: in a box, in bold type and in a font at least as large as the predominant font size of the document
in the footnotes
in italics in a smaller font
provided orally only
questions.explanation: Warning statements must be prominent: in a box, in bold, and in a font at least as large as the predominant font. This applied under CPC 2012 and continues under the revised Code.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 45; CPC 2012, Chapter 4

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, advertisements must be:
options: approved by the Central Bank before publication
published only in print media
clear, fair, accurate and not misleading
accompanied by the firm's full annual accounts
questions.explanation: The core advertising standard under both CPC 2012 and the revised Code is that advertisements are clear, fair, accurate and not misleading. Firms do not need prior Central Bank approval.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 77; CPC 2012, Chapter 9

questions.question: Which warning statement must an advertisement for an investment product whose value can fluctuate contain?
options: 'Warning: This product is guaranteed by the Central Bank.'
'Warning: Returns are fixed for the term.'
'Warning: Tax relief may change.'
'Warning: The value of your investment may go down as well as up.'
questions.explanation: Advertisements for investment products that can fall in value must carry this prescribed warning; other warnings, e.g. on past performance or loss of capital, apply where relevant.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 392; CPC 2012, Chapter 9

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), where an advertisement for an investment product quotes past performance, it must:
options: show the preceding 5 years (or the whole period since launch if shorter), based on actual performance, with the warning 'Past performance is not a reliable guide to future performance'
show only the best-performing year
show at least 10 years of simulated performance
omit any warning if performance has been positive
questions.explanation: Past performance figures must cover the preceding five years (or the full period if shorter), be based on actual performance, and carry the prescribed past performance warning.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), a firm receiving a written complaint must acknowledge it on paper or another durable medium within:
options: 1 working day
5 working days
10 working days
20 working days
questions.explanation: Complaints must be acknowledged within 5 working days (5 business days under CPC 2012); complaints made online should receive an immediate or automatic acknowledgement under the revised Code.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 105; CPC 2012, provision 10.9

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code's complaints procedure, a firm must give the complainant regular updates on the complaint at intervals of no more than:
options: 5 working days
10 working days
20 working days
40 working days
questions.explanation: Updates must be given at intervals of no more than 20 working days (business days under CPC 2012), and the firm should try to investigate and resolve the complaint within 40 working days.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 105; CPC 2012, provision 10.9

questions.question: Brian complained to his insurer 40 working days ago and the complaint is still not resolved. Under the Consumer Protection Code, what must the insurer do?
options: Close the complaint file automatically
Refer the complaint to the Central Bank
Pay Brian compensation
Tell Brian the expected timeframe for resolution and that he can refer the complaint to the relevant ombudsman (FSPO), giving contact details
questions.explanation: Firms should try to resolve complaints within 40 working days. If not resolved by then, the firm must tell the consumer the expected timeframe and of their right to refer the matter to the ombudsman.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 105; CPC 2012, provision 10.9

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), how often must a firm analyse patterns in its complaints and its errors, with reporting to compliance, risk and the board?
options: Every 5 years
Only when the Central Bank asks
At least every 6 months
Once every 3 years
questions.explanation: The revised Code requires analysis of both complaints and errors at least every 6 months, with reporting to compliance, risk and the board, to identify root causes and prevent recurrence.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), errors affecting consumers must be resolved speedily and no later than:
options: 5 working days after discovery
2 years after discovery
the end of the financial year
6 months after the date the error was discovered
questions.explanation: Firms must resolve errors speedily and within 6 months of discovery, including fixing systems, refunding affected consumers with interest where relevant, and notifying current and former affected consumers.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, where a conflict of interest cannot reasonably be avoided, the firm must:
options: disclose the conflict to the consumer, ensure it does not damage the consumer's interests, and obtain the consumer's written acknowledgement before proceeding
proceed without telling the consumer, provided it records the conflict
refuse to deal with the consumer in all cases
notify the FSPO
questions.explanation: Firms must have a conflicts policy and avoid conflicts where possible. Where unavoidable, the conflict must be disclosed, the consumer must not be disadvantaged, and the consumer's written acknowledgement obtained before proceeding.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Regs. 22-24; CPC 2012, Chapter 3

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), an intermediary may describe itself as 'independent' only where:
options: it is not owned by a bank
it holds agencies with at least five insurers

all its regulated activities are provided on the basis of a fair analysis of the market, and it does not accept or retain fees, commissions or other rewards from third parties when giving advice (other than minor non-monetary benefits)
it discloses all commissions in its terms of business
questions.explanation: Using 'independent' requires both a fair analysis of the market across all its regulated activities and not accepting or retaining third-party remuneration (apart from minor non-monetary benefits) - only fees paid by the consumer. Simply disclosing commission is not enough.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, records relating to a transaction must generally be retained for at least:
options: 6 years after the transaction is completed or discontinued
1 year
3 years
10 years from the date the customer was born
questions.explanation: Both CPC 2012 and the revised Code require transaction records to be kept for 6 years after the transaction ends; other records are kept for 6 years after the firm stops providing the service.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 117; CPC 2012, Chapter 11

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code 2012, how many unsolicited communications could a firm make to a borrower about arrears in a calendar month?
options: No more than one
No more than three
No more than five
There was no limit
questions.explanation: CPC 2012 limited unsolicited arrears communications to three per calendar month. The revised Code (2025) limits unsolicited arrears-related telephone calls to three per calendar month, with certain exclusions.
questions.reference: CPC 2012, Chapter 8; Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Reg. 279

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), what happened to the Code of Conduct on Mortgage Arrears (CCMA)?
options: It continues as a separate code alongside the revised CPC
It was abolished, and mortgage arrears are no longer specifically regulated
It was revoked, and its requirements, including the Mortgage Arrears Resolution Process (MARP), were incorporated into the Consumer Protection Regulations 2025
It was transferred to the FSPO
questions.explanation: The CCMA was revoked and its protections were brought into the Consumer Protection Regulations 2025 (Part 3, Chapter 9), which set out the MARP for mortgage arrears on a primary residence.

questions.question: Under the CCMA (and the revised CPC's mortgage arrears rules), the Mortgage Arrears Resolution Process (MARP) applies to arrears on a primary residence mortgage when the arrears:
options: first arise, even if paid the same day
reach €10,000
are referred to the FSPO
have persisted for 31 calendar days, or in pre-arrears cases where the borrower is in or likely to be in financial difficulty
questions.explanation: MARP applies when arrears persist for 31 calendar days from when they first arose, in pre-arrears cases, and where an alternative repayment arrangement is broken or expires. The lender must then notify the borrower within 3 working days.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Regulations 2025, Regs. 240 and 245; CCMA 2013

questions.question: Under the mortgage arrears rules (CCMA and the revised CPC), before starting legal proceedings for repossession against a co-operating borrower, a lender must generally wait until at least:
options: 8 months from the date arrears first arose (or 3 months after certain MARP decisions or notices, if later)
31 days from the date arrears first arose
3 months from the date arrears first arose
2 years from the date arrears first arose
questions.explanation: The '8-month rule' means a lender must wait at least 8 months from when arrears first arose, or 3 months after relevant decisions or information were given, whichever is later. It does not protect borrowers classified as not co-operating.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), once a claimant accepts a settlement offer, the insurer must pay the claim within:
options: 5 working days
30 calendar days
10 working days
3 months
questions.explanation: Settlement must be paid within 10 working days of the claimant's acceptance. Claimants must also be given at least 10 working days to consider a settlement offer, unless waived in writing.

questions.question: The ban on 'price walking' in home and motor insurance, now in the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), means that:
options: an insurer cannot charge a renewing customer more than the equivalent first-renewal price for that customer
all customers must pay exactly the same premium
premiums cannot increase at renewal for any reason
new customers must be charged more than renewing customers
questions.explanation: Differential pricing rules prevent insurers from charging long-standing customers more simply because of their tenure: the renewal price cannot exceed the equivalent first renewal price. Premiums can still change for genuine risk or cost reasons.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), when assessing affordability for a variable-rate mortgage, a lender must assess whether the borrower could still afford repayments if the interest rate increased by:
options: No rate increase needs to be considered
questions.explanation: Mortgage affordability must be stress-tested against a 2% rise in the interest rate. The test does not apply to fixed rates of 5 years or more.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), may a lender increase a personal consumer's credit card limit without being asked?
options: Yes, if the consumer has a good repayment record
Yes, if the increase is less than €1,000
No, a credit limit may not be increased without the personal consumer's prior written consent
Yes, provided the consumer is told within 30 days
questions.explanation: A credit limit cannot be increased without the personal consumer's prior written consent, and unsolicited pre-approved credit cannot be offered to personal consumers. CPC 2012 had similar restrictions.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), a bank may offer products as a bundle only where:
options: the consumer is an existing customer
the bundle includes a current account
the products are all from the same product producer
it can show that the bundle gives the consumer an overall cost saving
questions.explanation: Bundling is allowed only where an overall cost saving for the consumer can be shown, with the total cost and individual product costs disclosed. Contingent selling (forcing a purchase of another product) is generally prohibited.

questions.question: The revised Consumer Protection Code (2025) introduced a chapter on digitalisation. Which practice does it prohibit on a firm's digital platforms?
options: Pre-selected options or boxes confirming that the consumer has read or understood information
Allowing consumers to apply online
Providing a step-by-step guide
Displaying contact details for assistance
questions.explanation: The digitalisation rules ban pre-ticked boxes confirming that information has been read or understood, and require platforms to be easy to use, with clear step-by-step guidance and contact details displayed prominently.

questions.question: Under the revised Consumer Protection Code (2025), to which activity of a credit union do the Consumer Protection Regulations apply?
options: All lending activities
Only when the credit union acts as an insurance intermediary
All savings and lending activities
No activities of credit unions
questions.explanation: Credit unions are largely subject to their own regime under the Credit Union Act 1997; the Consumer Protection Regulations apply to them only when they act as insurance intermediaries.

questions.question: Under the GDPR, which of the following best describes 'personal data'?
options: Only information that is marked confidential by the organisation holding it
Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person
Any information about a person or a company that is stored electronically
Only information that would allow a person to be contacted, such as a name, address or phone number
questions.explanation: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual. It is not limited to contact details or electronic records, and data about a company as such is not personal data.

questions.question: Which of the following is 'special category' personal data under the GDPR?
options: A client's bank account and credit card details
A client's annual salary
Information about a client's health disclosed in a protection insurance application
A client's home address and date of birth
questions.explanation: Data concerning health is one of the special categories in Article 9. Financial information is sensitive in an everyday sense but is not a special category under the GDPR.

questions.question: Under the GDPR, a 'controller' is the person or body that:
options: determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data
processes personal data only on the documented instructions of another organisation
supervises compliance with the GDPR on behalf of a Member State
is the individual to whom the personal data relates
questions.explanation: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed. A processor acts on the controller's instructions, the supervisory authority oversees compliance, and the data subject is the individual concerned.

questions.question: A brokerage firm engages a cloud-based CRM provider to store and host its client files. The provider uses the data only to deliver the hosting service to the firm. Under the GDPR, the CRM provider is best described as:
options: a joint controller with the brokerage
a third party with no GDPR obligations
the data subject's representative
a processor, which must act under a written contract with the brokerage
questions.explanation: A provider that processes personal data on behalf of, and on the instructions of, the controller is a processor. Article 28 requires the processing to be governed by a binding contract setting out the processor's obligations.

questions.question: Which of the following activities counts as 'processing' of personal data under the GDPR?
options: Only collecting personal data for the first time
Any operation performed on personal data, including collection, storage, consultation, disclosure and erasure
Only using personal data to make an automated decision
Only transferring personal data to another organisation
questions.explanation: Processing is defined very widely and covers virtually anything done with personal data, from collection and storage through to consultation, disclosure and destruction.
