questions.question: A firm replaces client names in a spreadsheet with reference codes, but keeps a separate key file that links each code back to the client. Under the GDPR, the coded spreadsheet is:
options: anonymous data, so the GDPR no longer applies to it
special category data, because it has been altered
pseudonymised data, which is still personal data
outside the GDPR as long as the key file is stored in a different building
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data can be re-attributed to an individual using additional information, so it remains personal data. Only truly anonymised data, where individuals can no longer be identified, falls outside the GDPR.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the principles relating to processing of personal data set out in Article 5 of the GDPR?
options: Storage limitation
Profit maximisation
Freedom of information
Caveat emptor
questions.explanation: Storage limitation, meaning data is kept in identifiable form no longer than necessary, is one of the Article 5 principles alongside lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability.

questions.question: The GDPR 'accountability' principle requires a controller to:
options: obtain consent before any processing of personal data
appoint an external auditor to review its data protection compliance each year
report every data protection complaint to the Data Protection Commission
be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate, compliance with the data protection principles
questions.explanation: Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for compliance with the principles and requires it to be able to demonstrate that compliance, for example through policies, records and DPIAs. Consent is only one of several lawful bases.

questions.question: Ciarán, a QFA, uses a fact-find form that asks every pension client for their religion, the names of their neighbours and their social media passwords 'in case it is useful later'. Which principle is most clearly breached?
options: Accuracy
Data minimisation
Storage limitation
Integrity and confidentiality
questions.explanation: Data minimisation requires personal data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purpose. Collecting information with no link to the advice being given, just in case it is useful, breaches this principle.

questions.question: A firm collected clients' email addresses solely to send policy documents. It now wants to pass the list to an unrelated company for that company's own marketing, without telling the clients. Which principle is most directly engaged?
options: Purpose limitation
Accuracy
Data portability
Storage limitation
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation requires data to be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes. Disclosure to a third party for its own marketing is incompatible with the original purpose.

questions.question: A prospective client asks a broker for a quotation for life cover. Which lawful basis most naturally covers processing the client's details to prepare that quotation?
options: Vital interests of the data subject
Performance of a task carried out in the public interest
Processing necessary for a contract, including steps taken at the data subject's request before entering into it
Legitimate interests of a third party
questions.explanation: Article 6(1)(b) covers processing necessary for the performance of a contract or to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract, which includes preparing a requested quotation.

questions.question: A financial adviser copies a client's passport and proof of address to meet customer due diligence requirements under anti-money laundering law. The most appropriate lawful basis for this processing is:
options: consent, because the client handed over the documents voluntarily
legitimate interests, because the adviser wants to protect its reputation
vital interests, because money laundering harms society
compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject
questions.explanation: CDD is required by the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, so the processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation. Relying on consent would be inappropriate because the client cannot meaningfully refuse and still receive the service.

questions.question: A firm's online form contains a pre-ticked box stating 'I agree to receive marketing'. Under the GDPR, this is:
options: not valid consent, because consent requires a clear affirmative act by the data subject
valid consent, provided the client can untick the box
valid consent, provided the privacy notice mentions marketing
valid consent for existing clients but not for new clients
questions.explanation: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and an unambiguous indication of wishes by a statement or clear affirmative action. Silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity do not constitute consent.

questions.question: Where processing is based on consent, which statement about withdrawal is correct?
options: Consent can only be withdrawn in writing with 30 days' notice
Withdrawal makes all earlier processing unlawful from the outset
It must be as easy to withdraw consent as to give it, and withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing before withdrawal
Once given, consent cannot be withdrawn during the term of a contract
questions.explanation: Article 7(3) gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time, requires withdrawal to be as easy as giving consent, and confirms that withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal.

questions.question: An insurance intermediary needs to process an applicant's medical history to place income protection cover. Which statement best describes what the GDPR requires?
options: Only an Article 6 lawful basis is needed, as for any other data
Only an Article 9 condition is needed, because Article 9 replaces Article 6 for health data
No lawful basis is needed because the applicant volunteered the information
Both an Article 6 lawful basis and a condition under Article 9 (or a national derogation under it) are needed
questions.explanation: Processing of special category data is prohibited unless an Article 9(2) condition applies, and the processing must also have an Article 6 lawful basis. The Data Protection Act 2018 sets out additional Irish conditions made under Article 9, including for certain insurance and pension purposes.
questions.reference: GDPR Art. 6, Art. 9; Data Protection Act 2018

questions.question: In Ireland, what is the 'digital age of consent' set by the Data Protection Act 2018 for offering information society services directly to a child on the basis of consent?
questions.explanation: The GDPR allows Member States to set the age between 13 and 16. Ireland set it at 16, so below that age parental consent is required where consent is the lawful basis.
questions.reference: GDPR Art. 8; Data Protection Act 2018, s.31

questions.question: A client submits a subject access request to her broker. Within what period must the broker normally respond?
options: Without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months where necessary
Within 40 days of receipt, with no extension
Within 72 hours of receipt
Within three months of receipt in all cases
questions.explanation: The controller must respond without undue delay and at the latest within one month. This can be extended by two further months taking into account the complexity and number of requests, and the data subject must be told of any extension within the first month.

questions.question: Can a controller charge a fee for responding to a first subject access request?
options: Yes, a standard statutory fee applies to every request
Yes, the controller may charge whatever it costs to search its systems
No, unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, or for further copies a reasonable fee may be charged
No, and the controller may never charge a fee in any circumstances
questions.explanation: Information must generally be provided free of charge. A reasonable fee based on administrative costs may be charged for further copies, or where requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive (in which case the controller may alternatively refuse to act).

questions.question: A client tells his adviser that the date of birth on file is wrong and provides his birth certificate. Which right is the client exercising?
options: Right to restriction of processing
Right to data portability
Right to object
Right to rectification
questions.explanation: The right to rectification entitles a data subject to have inaccurate personal data corrected without undue delay, and incomplete data completed.

questions.question: Niamh, a former client, asks her financial adviser to erase all her records. The adviser completed her last transaction two years ago and is required by anti-money laundering law to keep the CDD and transaction records for five years. What is the correct approach?
options: Erase everything immediately, as the right to erasure is absolute
Retain the records required by law, because erasure does not apply to the extent processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation, and tell Niamh why
Refuse the request entirely and keep all her data indefinitely
Ask the Data Protection Commission for permission before deciding
questions.explanation: The right to erasure is not absolute: Article 17(3)(b) disapplies it where processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation. The adviser may keep what the AML rules require, should erase data not covered by an exemption, and must explain the decision to Niamh.

questions.question: A client contests the accuracy of income figures held on her file. While the firm verifies them, she asks that the data not be used. Which right allows this?
options: Right to restriction of processing
Right to erasure
Right to data portability
Right not to be subject to automated decision-making
questions.explanation: Where accuracy is contested, the data subject can require restriction for a period enabling the controller to verify the accuracy. Restricted data may be stored but generally not otherwise processed.

questions.question: The right to data portability applies where:
options: any personal data is held, whatever the lawful basis or format
the processing is based on legitimate interests and is carried out on paper
the processing is based on consent or on a contract and is carried out by automated means
the data subject has previously made a subject access request
questions.explanation: Portability covers personal data the data subject provided to the controller, where processing is based on consent or contract and is carried out by automated means. It entitles the data subject to receive the data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format.

questions.question: A client objects to her broker using her personal data for direct marketing. What must the broker do?
options: Continue unless it can show compelling legitimate grounds that override her interests
Stop processing her data for direct marketing purposes
Stop processing all of her data for every purpose, including servicing her policy
Refer the objection to the Data Protection Commission
questions.explanation: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute: once the data subject objects, the data must no longer be processed for that purpose. The 'compelling legitimate grounds' test applies to objections to other processing based on public task or legitimate interests.

questions.question: A lender's online system automatically declines loan applications with no human involvement. Under Article 22 GDPR, which statement is correct?
options: Fully automated decisions are always prohibited
Fully automated decisions are permitted in all cases provided a privacy notice is published
The data subject can only challenge the decision through the courts

Such decisions are permitted only on specified grounds such as necessity for a contract or explicit consent, with safeguards including the right to obtain human intervention and to contest the decision
questions.explanation: Data subjects have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal or similarly significant effects, unless it is necessary for a contract, authorised by law, or based on explicit consent. In the contract and consent cases the controller must provide safeguards, at least the right to human intervention, to express a view and to contest the decision.

questions.question: When must a controller give a data subject the information required by Article 13 GDPR (such as its identity, the purposes and lawful basis of processing, and retention periods) where the data is collected directly from that person?
options: At the time the personal data is obtained
Only if the data subject asks for it
Within one month after the data is obtained
Only at the end of the client relationship
questions.explanation: Where data is collected from the data subject, Article 13 information must be provided at the time the data is obtained, typically through a privacy notice. The one-month timeframe applies to data obtained from other sources under Article 14.

questions.question: In which of the following situations is the appointment of a Data Protection Officer mandatory under the GDPR?
options: Whenever an organisation has more than 50 employees
Whenever an organisation processes any customer data
Where the core activities of the controller consist of processing special category data on a large scale
Only where the Data Protection Commission directs it
questions.explanation: A DPO is mandatory for public authorities and bodies, and where core activities involve large-scale regular and systematic monitoring of individuals or large-scale processing of special category or criminal offence data. There is no employee-number threshold.

questions.question: Which statement about the position of a Data Protection Officer is correct?
options: The DPO is personally liable for any GDPR breach by the organisation
The DPO must not be dismissed or penalised for performing their tasks and reports to the highest management level
The DPO must be an external consultant and cannot be an employee
The DPO decides the purposes and means of processing on behalf of the controller
questions.explanation: The DPO must be independent in performing their tasks, must not be dismissed or penalised for doing so, and reports directly to the highest management level. Responsibility for compliance remains with the controller, and the DPO may be a staff member or a contractor.

questions.question: When must a controller carry out a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
options: After a personal data breach has occurred
Every year for all processing activities
Only when the data subject requests one
Before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals, particularly when using new technologies
questions.explanation: A DPIA is required prior to processing likely to result in a high risk. Where the DPIA shows high residual risk that the controller cannot mitigate, it must consult the Data Protection Commission before processing.

questions.question: Aoife, a QFA, accidentally emails a client's pension statement, showing his name, PPS number and fund value, to a different client. Under the GDPR this is best described as:
options: a personal data breach, because it is an unauthorised disclosure of personal data
not a breach, because it was accidental rather than malicious
not a breach, because no hacking or cyber-attack was involved
a breach only if the recipient actually reads the attachment
questions.explanation: A personal data breach is a breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data. Accidental misdirected emails are a very common type of breach.

questions.question: Where a personal data breach is likely to result in a risk to individuals, an Irish controller must notify the Data Protection Commission:
options: within 30 days
within one month
without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it
only if the affected individuals complain
questions.explanation: Article 33 requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach; a late notification must be accompanied by reasons for the delay.

questions.question: When must a controller communicate a personal data breach to the affected data subjects?
options: In every case, within 72 hours
Only when instructed to do so by An Garda Síochána
Never; notification to the supervisory authority is sufficient
Without undue delay, where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms
questions.explanation: Communication to data subjects is required where the breach is likely to result in a high risk, so they can take steps to protect themselves. Exceptions apply, for example where the data was encrypted so it is unintelligible to unauthorised persons.

questions.question: A controller assesses a breach and concludes it is unlikely to result in any risk to individuals. What does the GDPR require?
options: Nothing; the breach can be disregarded
The controller need not notify the DPC, but must still document the breach, its effects and the remedial action taken
The controller must notify the DPC within 72 hours regardless
The controller must notify all its clients
questions.explanation: Notification to the supervisory authority is not required where the breach is unlikely to result in a risk, but Article 33(5) requires all breaches to be documented so the supervisory authority can verify compliance.

questions.question: A processor discovers a breach affecting data it holds for a controller. What must the processor do?
options: Notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of the breach
Notify the DPC directly within 72 hours instead of telling the controller
Notify the affected data subjects directly
Nothing, because only controllers have breach obligations
questions.explanation: Under Article 33(2) the processor must notify the controller without undue delay. The controller then decides on notification to the supervisory authority and data subjects.

questions.question: An Irish broker wants to use a back-office provider that will store client data in a country outside the EEA. Which of the following can provide a lawful basis for that transfer?
options: The provider's assurance by phone that it takes data protection seriously
A European Commission adequacy decision for that country, or appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses
The fact that the provider is a large multinational company
Registration of the transfer with the Companies Registration Office
questions.explanation: Transfers outside the EEA are permitted on the basis of an adequacy decision, or appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules, or (narrowly) specific derogations. Informal assurances are not sufficient.

questions.question: Which body is the supervisory authority responsible for monitoring the application of the GDPR in Ireland?
options: The Central Bank of Ireland
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
The Data Protection Commission
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
questions.explanation: The Data Protection Act 2018 established the Data Protection Commission as Ireland's supervisory authority for the GDPR.

questions.question: Which of the following is a corrective power of a supervisory authority such as the Data Protection Commission under Article 58 GDPR?
options: Revoking a firm's authorisation from the Central Bank
Sentencing company directors to imprisonment
Awarding compensation directly to individual data subjects
Imposing a temporary or definitive limitation, including a ban, on processing
questions.explanation: Article 58(2) corrective powers include warnings, reprimands, orders to comply, bans or limitations on processing, suspension of data flows and administrative fines. Compensation for data subjects is a matter for the courts, and authorisation is a Central Bank function.

questions.question: For an infringement of the basic principles for processing (including conditions for consent) or of data subjects' rights, the maximum administrative fine for an undertaking under the GDPR is:
options: up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
up to €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
up to €20 million or 4% of Irish turnover, whichever is lower
a fixed fine of €1 million
questions.explanation: Article 83(5) sets the higher tier at €20m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for breaches of principles, lawful basis, consent, data subject rights and transfer rules. The €10m/2% tier in Article 83(4) applies to obligations such as security, breach notification, DPIAs and DPOs.

questions.question: Under the Data Protection Act 2018, what is the maximum administrative fine the DPC may impose on a public authority or public body that does not act as an undertaking?
options: Public bodies cannot be fined at all
questions.explanation: Section 141 of the Data Protection Act 2018 caps administrative fines on public authorities and bodies (other than those acting as undertakings) at €1 million.

questions.question: Under the ePrivacy Regulations 2011 (S.I. 336 of 2011), a broker may send a marketing email about its own products to an existing individual client without fresh consent where, among other conditions:
options: the client has not complained about previous emails
the email is sent only on a weekday during business hours
the contact details were obtained in the context of a sale, the client was given an opt-out at collection and in each message, and the first marketing email is sent within 12 months of the sale
the broker includes its Central Bank authorisation number in the email
questions.explanation: Regulation 13(11) provides a limited existing-customer exemption. The DPC's guidance lists the conditions: details obtained in the context of a sale, marketing of the firm's own products or services, a free and simple opt-out at collection and in every message, and the first marketing message sent within 12 months of the sale.
questions.reference: S.I. 336 of 2011, Reg. 13(11); DPC guidance on electronic direct marketing

questions.question: Which approach to retaining client files best complies with the GDPR storage limitation principle?
options: Keep all client files permanently in case of future disputes
Delete client files as soon as each sale is completed
Keep files only for as long as the client remains alive
Set documented retention periods based on legal and regulatory requirements and genuine business need, and securely delete or anonymise data when they expire
questions.explanation: Personal data must be kept in identifiable form no longer than necessary for the purposes. A documented retention schedule, linked to statutory requirements such as AML record keeping, supports compliance; indefinite retention and premature deletion both create problems.

questions.question: From what date did the Minimum Competency Code 2017 and the Minimum Competency Regulations 2017 replace the Minimum Competency Code 2011?
options: 1 January 2017
3 January 2018
1 October 2018
21 March 2019
questions.explanation: MCC 2017 and the MCR 2017 took effect from 3 January 2018, the same date MiFID II applied. 21 March 2019 was the deadline for grandfathered mortgage staff to qualify.

questions.question: Under which legal powers were the MCC 2017 Standards and the Minimum Competency Regulations 2017 respectively issued?
options: Both under section 48 of the Central Bank (Supervision and Enforcement) Act 2013
Both under the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
The MCC under section 50 of the Central Bank Reform Act 2010; the Regulations under section 48 of the Central Bank (Supervision and Enforcement) Act 2013
The MCC under the Consumer Credit Act 1995; the Regulations under the Central Bank Act 1942
questions.explanation: The MCC's standards are Fitness and Probity standards issued under s.50 of the 2010 Act, which is why MCC compliance links into the F&P regime. The MCR 2017 impose obligations on firms under s.48 of the 2013 Act.
questions.reference: MCC 2017, Part 1, s.1.1; MCC/MCR Q&A, Q1.1

questions.question: What is the main aim of the Minimum Competency Code?
options: To set capital requirements for intermediaries
To set maximum commission levels for advisers
To regulate the advertising of financial products
To ensure consumers get a minimum acceptable level of competence from individuals advising on or dealing with retail financial products
questions.explanation: The MCC sets minimum professional standards for people providing certain financial services, particularly to consumers, so consumers receive a minimum acceptable level of competence.
questions.reference: Central Bank MCC webpage; MCC 2017, Introduction

questions.question: Part 1 of the MCC 2017 applies to persons exercising a controlled function on a professional basis that includes which activity (outside MiFID services)?
options: Providing advice or information to consumers on retail financial products, or arranging or offering to arrange them
Preparing a firm's statutory accounts
Maintaining a firm's IT systems
Recruiting staff for a regulated firm
questions.explanation: Section 1.2 covers advising or giving information to consumers on retail financial products, arranging or offering to arrange them (including amending insurance cover and restructuring loans), and certain specified functions.

questions.question: A bank employee's only involvement with travel insurance is that it is provided free of charge with a premium current account. Does the MCC apply to that employee in respect of the travel insurance?
options: Yes, because travel insurance is a retail financial product
No, because the standards do not apply where a person deals solely with a retail financial product provided free of charge in conjunction with another financial product
Yes, but only if the employee is a PCF holder
No, because the MCC never applies to bank staff
questions.explanation: Section 1.2 states that the standards do not apply to a controlled function concerned solely with providing a retail financial product free of charge in conjunction with another financial product.

questions.question: Under Appendix 1 of MCC 2017, in which category of retail financial product does a PRSA fall?
options: Savings and Investments
Life Assurance
Consumer Credit Agreements
Pensions
questions.explanation: The Pensions category includes personal pension plans, PRSAs, AVCs and ARFs/AMRFs secured by assurance contracts, annuities and buy-out bonds.

questions.question: Which of the following is EXCLUDED from the 'Consumer Credit Agreements and Associated Insurances' category of retail financial products in MCC 2017?
options: Credit cards
Hire-purchase agreements
Personal cash loans
Payment protection insurance sold with a personal loan
questions.explanation: Appendix 1 excludes moneylending agreements, housing loans and mortgage credit agreements, credit cards, overdrafts and overrunning from this category. Cash loans, hire purchase and associated PPI are included.

questions.question: For firms not regulated under MiFID II, which deposits are listed as retail financial products under 'Other Savings and Investments' in MCC 2017?
options: All demand deposit accounts
Deposits with a term of one year or more
Only deposits over €100,000
Only deposits in foreign currencies
questions.explanation: Appendix 1 lists 'deposits with a term equal to or greater than one year' under Other Savings and Investments, alongside life savings policies, collective investment schemes, transferable securities and tracker bonds.

questions.question: Which of the following is a 'specified function' under Appendix 2 of MCC 2017?
options: Processing direct debit instructions in a back office
Managing the firm's IT security
Adjudicating on a consumer complaint about advice on a retail financial product
Preparing the firm's marketing budget
questions.explanation: Specified functions include assisting with and deciding insurance claims, debt management services, directly managing or supervising advisers, adjudicating complaints, reinsurance distribution, being on the board of a mortgage credit intermediary, and product design.

questions.question: The Qualified Financial Adviser (QFA) designation is a recognised qualification under MCC 2017 for which categories of retail financial product?
options: Life assurance, pensions, savings and investments, mortgage credit/housing loans and consumer credit
Personal and commercial general insurance only
All eight categories, including personal and commercial general insurance
Pensions only
questions.explanation: Appendix 4 lists the QFA for life assurance, pensions, savings and investments, mortgages/housing loans and consumer credit. General insurance categories are covered by qualifications such as the Certified Insurance Practitioner (CIP).

questions.question: Niamh will advise consumers on household and private motor insurance. Which of these qualifications is recognised for personal general insurance under MCC 2017?
options: Registered Stockbroker
Certified Insurance Practitioner (CIP)
Accredited Product Adviser (Loans)
Diploma in Life and Disability Claims
questions.explanation: The CIP (Insurance Institute of Ireland) is recognised for personal general, commercial general and private medical insurance. The other options relate to investments, loans or life claims.

questions.question: What role does the Central Bank play in relation to recognised qualifications under the MCC?
options: It designs the courses and sets the examinations
It marks the examinations of new entrants
It sets and reviews the Standards and confirms whether a qualification meets them; it does not take part in course design or examinations
It awards the QFA designation
questions.explanation: Section 3.1 of the MCC states the Central Bank does not take part in course design or examinations; its role is to set the Standards and formally recognise qualifications that meet them.

questions.question: To be recognised by the Central Bank under the MCC, a new qualification must, among other things:
options: be offered only by a university
be examinable only in Irish
require at least 30 CPD hours a year
be included in the National Framework of Qualifications at Level 7 or higher and include CPD requirements with at least one hour of ethics
questions.explanation: Section 3.3 requires broad industry support, coverage of the Appendix 3 competencies, an equivalent standard to existing qualifications, NFQ Level 7 or higher, and ongoing CPD (not materially different from the MCC) with an ethics module of at least one hour.

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, what is the maximum total period for which a new entrant may take part in the training process?
options: Two years
Four years
Three years
Five years
questions.explanation: Section 1.4(e) sets the maximum period in the training process at four years in total, subject to pro-rata adjustment in limited circumstances such as statutory leave or serious illness.

questions.question: Conor is a new entrant giving information on mortgages. Under MCC 2017, which of the following must apply to him?
options: He may work unsupervised once he has passed one exam module
He must hold a recognised qualification before speaking to any consumer
He must act under the direction and supervision of a qualified person, and his documentation must be checked and approved in writing by a person who meets the Standards
He must be supervised only by the Central Bank
questions.explanation: New entrants must complete initial training (or part of a recognised qualification), act under the immediate direction and supervision of a nominated person who meets the Standards, and have documentation checked and approved in writing until they qualify.

questions.question: In relation to exams, a new entrant under MCC 2017 must:
options: sit all exams within the first six months
complete the qualification in any order, at any pace, within ten years
postpone exams until after one year's experience
register for the first available sitting of the relevant exam they could reasonably be expected to sit, and each available sitting after that until they qualify
questions.explanation: Section 1.4(c) requires new entrants to register for the first available sitting, keep working towards the qualification on a consistent and timely basis, and keep a record of exams completed, results and exams scheduled.

questions.question: In which situation may the four-year new entrant timeframe be adjusted pro rata under MCC 2017?
options: Statutory maternity leave, provided the person does not carry out relevant functions during it
Working part-time
Taking annual holidays
A period of unemployment
questions.explanation: Pro-rata adjustment may apply for statutory leave (maternity, adoption, parental), serious illness of at least two months (medically certified) and, for new entrants, a career break. It does not apply to part-time work, unemployment, retirement or holidays.

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, a new entrant providing MiFID services or activities must keep written records of relevant experience in which format?
options: A personal diary reviewed annually by the Central Bank
The Certificate of Experience set out in Appendix 5 of the Code, signed on behalf of the regulated firm
A statutory declaration sworn before a solicitor
No records are needed if the person holds a recognised qualification
questions.explanation: MiFID staff need a recognised qualification plus at least six months' relevant experience on a full-time equivalent basis. New entrants providing MiFID services must record their experience using the Appendix 5 Certificate of Experience.
questions.reference: MCC 2017, s.1.4(d) and Appendix 5; MCC/MCR Q&A, Q4.2

questions.question: For which of the following can a person NOT rely on grandfathering under MCC 2017?
options: Advising on life assurance protection policies
Advising on personal general insurance
MiFID services or activities
Advising on pensions
questions.explanation: Grandfathering is not available for functions relating to debt management services, mortgage credit agreements (after 21 March 2019) or MiFID services and activities. For other products, eligible persons may still rely on it.

questions.question: For most retail financial products, which date was relevant to whether a person could be grandfathered under the minimum competency regime?
options: The person was dealing with the product on 3 January 2018
The person was dealing with the product on 21 March 2019
The person was dealing with the product on 1 October 2024
The person was dealing with the product on 1 January 2007
questions.explanation: Grandfathering required the person to have been dealing with the product on 1 January 2007 (1 June 2008 for retail credit and home reversion agreements), with the required prior experience, a documented firm assessment and certification, and ongoing CPD.

questions.question: A mortgage adviser had been grandfathered for housing loans. Under the Mortgage Credit Regulations and MCC 2017, what was required?
options: The adviser needed a recognised qualification by 21 March 2019, or else could act only as a new entrant under supervision
Nothing; grandfathering for mortgages continues indefinitely
The adviser had to stop advising on mortgages permanently
The adviser needed Central Bank pre-approval as a PCF
questions.explanation: From 21 March 2019, knowledge and competence for mortgage credit could not be based solely on experience, so grandfathered staff needed a recognised qualification by then or had to act as new entrants under supervision.
questions.reference: MCC 2017, s.1.3 and s.1.5; MCC/MCR Q&A, Q5.2

questions.question: A person subject to Part 1 of MCC 2017 holds a recognised qualification whose ongoing maintenance does not depend on CPD. How many hours of CPD must they complete each year?
options: 10 hours
20 hours
15 hours
No CPD is required
questions.explanation: Section 1.7.1(b) requires 15 hours of CPD each year. Holders of a designation that itself depends on CPD (such as QFA) comply by meeting that designation's CPD requirements.

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, what is the minimum CPD each year that must relate to ethics?
options: Half an hour
Two hours
Five hours
One hour
questions.explanation: Section 1.7.1(f) requires at least one hour of CPD each year relating to ethics. More is allowed, but CPD overall must cover a range of competencies relevant to the person's role.
questions.reference: MCC 2017, Part 1, s.1.7.1(f); MCC/MCR Q&A, Q10.5

questions.question: Aoife, a QFA, advises on both pensions and mortgages. Apart from the ethics requirement, what does MCC 2017 require in relation to the content of her CPD?
options: At least one hour of CPD each year for each function within scope that she undertakes
All of her CPD must relate to pensions
She may choose any business topic, such as general management
At least eight hours on each product
questions.explanation: Section 1.7.1(e) requires at least one hour of CPD each year for each function undertaken within scope, and CPD content must be directly relevant to her functions and the Appendix 3 competencies.

questions.question: Ronan completed 22 hours of CPD in 2025. How many of the surplus hours can he carry into 2026 under MCC 2017?
options: All 7 hours
None
Up to 3 hours
Up to 5 hours
questions.explanation: Section 1.7.1(g) states that surplus hours in one year may not be carried into the following year.

questions.question: Gráinne completed only 11 hours of CPD last year. She has had no CPD shortfall in the previous five years. Under MCC 2017:
options: she is automatically struck off the firm's register
she must make up the shortfall within three months
she may make up the 4-hour shortfall by the end of the following year, in addition to that year's normal requirement
the shortfall is ignored because it is her first
questions.explanation: Under s.1.7.1(h), a shortfall may be made up by the end of the following year (on top of that year's requirement), provided there has been no other shortfall within the past five years.

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, what is the maximum number of CPD hours that can be counted in any one day, and for any single topic in a day?
options: Six hours a day; three hours per topic
Ten hours a day; five hours per topic
No daily limit applies
Eight hours a day; four hours per topic
questions.explanation: Section 1.7.2 caps CPD at eight hours in any day and four hours for any single topic in a day. CPD must also be accredited by a provider of a recognised qualification or a relevant professional educational body.

questions.question: Which statement about CPD hours under MCC 2017 is correct?
options: CPD hours must be accredited by the provider of a recognised qualification or a professional educational body providing recognised qualifications with a CPD requirement
Any training organised by the employer counts automatically
CPD hours must be approved in advance by the Central Bank
Only exam-based learning counts as CPD
questions.explanation: Section 1.7.2 requires all CPD hours to be accredited by a recognised qualification provider or a relevant professional educational body. CPD can be gained through seminars, lectures, conferences, e-learning, workshops or courses.

questions.question: According to the Central Bank's MCC Q&A, can a module on diversity, equity and inclusion count towards a person's MCC CPD requirement?
options: Yes, it counts as the ethics hour
No, because it relates to the general operation of the firm rather than the technical competencies in Appendix 3
Yes, up to a maximum of four hours
Only for PCF holders
questions.explanation: The Central Bank considers DEI topics important but not part of the Appendix 3 competencies, so they do not meet MCC CPD requirements. CPD content must relate to the competencies for the person's retail financial products.

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, in which circumstance can the annual CPD requirement be reduced pro rata?
options: The person works a three-day week
The person takes a career break
The person is out of work due to long-term illness of at least two months, with medical certification
The person takes their annual holidays
questions.explanation: Pro-rata CPD adjustment applies for statutory leave and serious illness (at least two months, medically certified). It does not apply for part-time work, unemployment, retirement, career breaks or holidays.

questions.question: Emma works in a call centre and gives information on a simple product strictly from a prescribed script. Under MCC 2017, which requirement applies to her?
options: She must hold a recognised qualification before taking any calls
She may answer any question the consumer raises, including questions outside the script
She does not need any training
The script must be devised by a person who meets the Standards, and she must refer requests outside the script to such a person
questions.explanation: A prescribed script function operates within narrow, rigid criteria. The person must use a script devised by a qualified person, complete firm training and ongoing training, refer out-of-script questions to a qualified person, and work under supervision.

questions.question: Under the Minimum Competency Regulations 2017, a regulated firm must:
options: establish and maintain a register of the accredited persons for whom it is responsible, including new entrants
publish the CPD records of all its staff on its website
submit every staff member's exam results to the Central Bank monthly
obtain Central Bank approval before hiring a new entrant
questions.explanation: The MCR 2017 require firms to keep a register of accredited persons (with details such as, for new entrants, start dates and the qualification being pursued), and impose related supervision, monitoring and record-keeping duties.

questions.question: The Minimum Competency Regulations 2017 introduced a requirement for firms to carry out an annual review. What is its purpose?
options: To certify each adviser's investment performance
To consider staff members' development and experience needs, qualifications, regulatory developments and new products offered by the firm
To report each staff member's CPD hours to the Central Bank
To renew each adviser's QFA designation
questions.explanation: The annual review aims to take account of staff development and experience needs, qualifications, regulatory developments and new retail financial products. The results need not be recorded on the MCC register, though the register may need updating afterwards.

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, a regulated firm may permit a person to perform a controlled function within scope only if:
options: the person has worked in financial services for at least ten years
the Central Bank has interviewed the person
the firm is satisfied on reasonable grounds that the person complies with the Standards and the person has agreed to abide by them
the person has a third-level degree
questions.explanation: Section 1.1 of the MCC states that a firm must not permit a person to perform a controlled function unless satisfied on reasonable grounds that the person complies with the Standards and has agreed to abide by them.

questions.question: From 1 October 2024, the MCC 2017 applies to all in-scope credit union services, such as lending and term deposits. What transitional arrangement applies to credit union staff in situ on that date?
options: They are grandfathered permanently
They have one year to qualify
They are exempt if they are volunteers
They have until 1 October 2028 to obtain a relevant recognised qualification
questions.explanation: The Central Bank allowed a four-year transition to 1 October 2028 for those in situ; there is no grandfathering for these credit union activities, and the MCC applies to volunteers and employees alike. New entrants follow s.1.4.
questions.reference: MCC/MCR Q&A, Q11.1, Q11.3 and Q12.2

questions.question: As of 2026, how has the scope of the MCC 2017 changed in relation to crypto-assets?
options: From 28 July 2026, it applies to staff of crypto-asset service providers who give information or advice on crypto-assets, in line with ESMA's MiCA guidelines
Crypto-assets were added as a category for which the QFA is automatically recognised
Crypto-asset staff may be grandfathered based on previous experience
The MCC does not apply to crypto-asset service providers
questions.explanation: The MCC was revised (June 2026 addendum) so that from 28 July 2026 it applies to CASP staff giving information (minimum 10 CPD hours a year) or advice (minimum 20 CPD hours a year) on crypto-assets. There is no grandfathering, but there are transitional arrangements for experienced staff.

questions.question: Under Part 2 of MCC 2017, a board member of a mortgage credit intermediary who is not in a consumer-facing role must complete how much CPD each year relating to mortgage credit?
options: 15 hours
6 hours
1 hour
None
questions.explanation: Section 2.2.2 requires six hours of CPD each year on mortgage credit agreements for these board members. If they are also consumer-facing, the 15-hour requirement applies and covers both roles.
questions.reference: MCC 2017, Part 2, s.2.2.2; MCC/MCR Q&A, Q10.3

questions.question: Under MCC 2017, what competency standard applies to the design of retail financial products?
options: Every member of the product design team must hold a recognised qualification
Product designers are outside the scope of the MCC
At least one key person in the product design decision-making process must meet the Standards for that product
The firm's CEO must hold the QFA
questions.explanation: Section 2.2.4 requires at least one key person with material influence in the product design decision-making process to meet the s.1.3(a) and (e) Standards (qualification and CPD) for that product.
questions.reference: MCC 2017, Part 2, s.2.2.4; MCC/MCR Q&A, Q6.1-6.2

questions.question: An Irish-registered insurance intermediary provides services in Germany on a freedom of services basis. According to the Central Bank's MCC Q&A, which competency standards are appropriate for those services?
options: The MCC 2017 in full, with no reference to German rules
No competency standards apply to passported services
Those set by EIOPA directly
The corresponding requirements of Germany, though the firm must still be able to show the Central Bank it meets IDD knowledge and competence requirements, including 15 hours of CPD a year
questions.explanation: For services provided in another EU/EEA state on a freedom of services or establishment basis, the Central Bank considers the host state's competency standards appropriate, but under IDD Article 10 firms must still demonstrate compliance, including 15 CPD hours a year.

questions.question: From 1 January 2025, the Central Bank amended the competencies in Appendix 3 of the MCC for all retail financial products to include:
options: cyber-security risk management
sustainability, including taking account of customers' sustainability preferences in suitability
anti-money laundering for board members only
artificial intelligence system design
questions.explanation: Sustainability competencies were added for all retail financial products, effective 1 January 2025, reflecting MiFID II and IDD suitability rules on sustainability preferences. AI and IT/cyber risks are not Appendix 3 competencies.

questions.question: From what date did MiFID II and MiFIR apply across the EU?
options: 1 November 2007
3 January 2018
1 January 2023
questions.explanation: MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) and MiFIR (Regulation (EU) No 600/2014) applied from 3 January 2018, replacing the original MiFID which applied from 1 November 2007. 25 May 2018 is the GDPR date.
questions.reference: Directive 2014/65/EU, Art. 93 (as amended by Directive (EU) 2016/1034); Regulation (EU) No 600/2014, Art. 55

questions.question: Which Irish statutory instrument transposed MiFID II into Irish law?
options: The Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
The Consumer Protection Code
The Data Protection Act 2018
The European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017
questions.explanation: MiFID II was transposed by the European Union (Markets in Financial Instruments) Regulations 2017 (S.I. No. 375 of 2017). The Investment Intermediaries Act 1995 governs non-MiFID investment intermediaries.

questions.question: What is the key legal difference between MiFID II and MiFIR?
options: MiFID II is a directive that had to be transposed into national law, while MiFIR is a regulation that applies directly in Member States
MiFID II applies only to banks, while MiFIR applies only to brokers
MiFIR is a directive and MiFID II is a regulation
MiFIR applies only outside the EU
questions.explanation: MiFID II is a directive transposed in Ireland by the 2017 Regulations, whereas MiFIR is directly applicable. MiFIR deals largely with transparency, transaction reporting and trading obligations.

questions.question: Which of the following is a 'financial instrument' under MiFID II?
options: A residential mortgage loan
Units in a collective investment undertaking
A unit-linked life assurance policy
A standard household insurance policy
questions.explanation: Units in collective investment undertakings are listed in Section C of Annex I. Unit-linked life policies are insurance-based investment products governed by the IDD, and mortgages and general insurance are outside MiFID.

questions.question: Which of the following is an 'investment service or activity' under MiFID II?
options: Arranging a home insurance policy
Providing a personal loan
Accepting a savings deposit
Reception and transmission of orders in relation to one or more financial instruments
questions.explanation: Section A of Annex I lists the investment services and activities, including reception and transmission of orders, execution of orders, dealing on own account, portfolio management, investment advice, underwriting and placing, and operating an MTF or OTF.

questions.question: Orla, a QFA, recommends a unit-linked investment bond issued by an Irish life assurance company. Which regime primarily governs the suitability and conduct requirements for this sale?
options: The Insurance Distribution Directive (IDD) regime for insurance-based investment products
MiFID II, because the bond invests in funds
The PRIIPs Regulation alone, with no conduct rules
No regime applies because the product is insurance
questions.explanation: Insurance-based investment products are excluded from MiFID II's conduct rules and are instead governed by the IDD (in Ireland, the European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018), which has its own suitability and conflicts requirements. A PRIIPs KID is still required, but that is a disclosure rule.

questions.question: Under the Article 3 optional exemption, as applied in Ireland to retail intermediaries authorised under the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995, which condition must be met for a firm to remain outside full MiFID authorisation?
options: The firm may hold client money provided it is segregated
The firm may execute orders on its own behalf in any financial instrument

The firm must not hold client funds or securities, and may only receive and transmit orders in transferable securities and units of collective investment undertakings and/or give investment advice on them, transmitting orders only to authorised entities such as MiFID firms or UCITS management companies
The firm must have fewer than ten employees
questions.explanation: Article 3 allows Member States to exempt firms that do not hold client funds or securities, are limited to RTO and/or advice in transferable securities and units of collective investment undertakings, and transmit orders only to specified authorised entities. Such firms must be subject to national requirements at least analogous to key MiFID requirements.

questions.question: Under MiFID II, clients are categorised into which three categories?
options: Personal, business and institutional clients
Retail clients, professional clients and eligible counterparties
Consumers, sophisticated investors and high-net-worth investors
Private clients, corporate clients and public clients
questions.explanation: MiFID II uses three categories with decreasing levels of protection: retail clients, professional clients (per se or elective) and eligible counterparties.

questions.question: Which client category receives the highest level of regulatory protection under MiFID II?
options: Eligible counterparties
Per se professional clients
Retail clients
Elective professional clients
questions.explanation: Retail clients receive the full range of conduct of business protections. Professional clients receive fewer, and eligible counterparties fewer still.

questions.question: A company is treated as a per se professional client as a 'large undertaking' if it meets at least two of three size requirements on a company basis. Which set lists those requirements correctly?
options: Balance sheet total of €5m; net turnover of €10m; own funds of €500,000
More than 250 employees; turnover of €50m; balance sheet of €43m
Balance sheet total of €43m; net turnover of €50m; own funds of €5m
Balance sheet total of €20m; net turnover of €40m; own funds of €2m
questions.explanation: Annex II treats large undertakings meeting two of the following as per se professional: balance sheet total of €20m, net turnover of €40m and own funds of €2m. The 250 employees / €50m / €43m figures are the EU SME definition thresholds.

questions.question: Brian, a retail client, asks to be treated as an elective professional client. He has a financial instrument portfolio, including cash deposits, of €650,000 and has worked for two years in a professional role in the financial sector requiring knowledge of the relevant transactions. Under the MiFID II quantitative test, which statement is correct?
options: He meets two of the three criteria, so the firm may treat him as professional if it also assesses his expertise and follows the required procedure
He cannot opt up because he does not meet all three criteria
He automatically becomes a professional client because his portfolio exceeds €500,000
He can only opt up to eligible counterparty status
questions.explanation: At least two of three criteria must be met: about 10 significant transactions per quarter over the previous four quarters; a portfolio exceeding €500,000; or at least one year in a relevant professional position in the financial sector. The firm must also assess expertise, give a written warning of lost protections, and receive the client's written statement.

questions.question: A per se professional client wants a higher level of protection. Under MiFID II, which statement is correct?
options: Once professional, a client can never be treated as retail
The client may request treatment as a retail client, and the firm may agree to provide the higher level of protection
Only the Central Bank can recategorise a client
The client can only be recategorised as an eligible counterparty
questions.explanation: A per se professional client may request non-professional treatment (opting down), and the firm can agree to provide a higher level of protection, either generally or for particular services, instruments or transactions. It is the client's responsibility to ask.

questions.question: Eligible counterparty status is relevant only when a firm provides which services?
options: Investment advice and portfolio management
Any investment service whatsoever
Safekeeping of financial instruments only
Execution of orders on behalf of clients, dealing on own account, and reception and transmission of orders
questions.explanation: Article 30 disapplies most conduct rules for these three services where the counterparty is an eligible counterparty. When providing investment advice or portfolio management, such a client is treated as a professional client.

questions.question: The MiFID II suitability assessment must be carried out when a firm provides:
options: investment advice or portfolio management
execution-only services in non-complex instruments
reception and transmission of orders without advice
safekeeping of financial instruments
questions.explanation: Suitability applies to investment advice and portfolio management. For other, non-advised services the appropriateness test generally applies instead, unless the execution-only conditions are met.

questions.question: When carrying out a suitability assessment, what information must the firm obtain from the client?
options: Knowledge and experience only
Investment objectives only
Knowledge and experience in the investment field, financial situation including ability to bear losses, and investment objectives including risk tolerance
Only the information the client volunteers
questions.explanation: Article 25(2) requires the firm to obtain information on the client's knowledge and experience, financial situation including ability to bear losses, and investment objectives including risk tolerance, so it can recommend services and instruments that are suitable.

questions.question: How does the appropriateness test differ from the suitability test?
options: Appropriateness is stricter, covering financial situation and objectives as well as knowledge
Appropriateness considers only whether the client has the knowledge and experience to understand the risks of the product or service
Appropriateness applies only to professional clients
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: For non-advised services, the appropriateness test assesses the client's knowledge and experience relevant to the specific product or service. It does not consider financial situation or objectives, which are part of suitability.

questions.question: In a non-advised sale, a retail client declines to provide information about her investment knowledge and experience. What must the firm do under MiFID II?
options: Refuse to deal with her under any circumstances
Treat her as a professional client
Proceed silently, because appropriateness is optional
Warn her that this decision will not allow the firm to determine whether the product or service is appropriate for her
questions.explanation: Under Article 25(3), if the client does not provide the information, or provides insufficient information, the firm must warn the client that it cannot determine appropriateness. The warning may be in a standardised format. By contrast, without the necessary information a firm must not make a personal recommendation.

questions.question: A firm may provide execution-only services without assessing appropriateness when, among other conditions:
options: the service relates to non-complex instruments and is provided at the client's initiative, and the client is informed that appropriateness will not be assessed
the client is a retail client investing less than €15,000
the instrument is a derivative traded on a regulated market
the firm has previously provided advice to the client on another product
questions.explanation: Article 25(4) permits execution-only where the service relates to listed non-complex instruments, is provided at the client's initiative, the client is clearly informed that appropriateness will not be assessed, and the firm complies with its conflicts obligations.

questions.question: Which of the following is generally treated as a complex instrument under MiFID II, so it cannot be sold on an execution-only basis?
options: Shares in a company admitted to trading on a regulated market (not embedding a derivative)
A money market instrument without an embedded derivative
An option or other derivative
Units in a non-structured UCITS
questions.explanation: Derivatives are complex. Shares admitted to trading on a regulated market (excluding shares in non-UCITS collective investment undertakings and shares embedding a derivative), money market instruments without embedded derivatives and non-structured UCITS units are among the instruments listed as non-complex.

questions.question: When providing investment advice to a retail client, when must a MiFID firm normally provide the statement on suitability?
options: Within one month after the transaction
Before the transaction is made
Only if the client requests it
At the next annual review
questions.explanation: Article 25(6) requires a suitability statement specifying the advice given and how it meets the client's preferences, objectives and other characteristics to be provided before the transaction. A limited exception allows it immediately afterwards for distance communication, if the client consents and is offered the option to delay.

questions.question: A MiFID firm informs clients that its investment advice is provided on an 'independent' basis. Which requirement applies?
options: It may accept commission from product providers provided it discloses the amount
It may only recommend products issued by entities with close links to the firm

It must assess a sufficiently diverse range of financial instruments available on the market and must not accept and retain fees, commissions or other monetary or non-monetary benefits from third parties, other than acceptable minor non-monetary benefits
It must charge the client a fixed fee of no more than 1% of assets
questions.explanation: Independent advice requires assessment of a sufficiently diverse range of instruments, not limited to the firm's own or closely linked providers, and a ban on accepting and retaining third-party inducements other than disclosed minor non-monetary benefits. Any monetary payments received must be passed to the client.

questions.question: Under MiFID II, a firm providing non-independent advice may receive a commission from a product provider only if the payment:
options: does not exceed 3% of the amount invested
is approved in advance by the Central Bank
is paid by the client rather than the provider

is designed to enhance the quality of the service to the client, does not impair the firm's duty to act in the client's best interests, and is clearly disclosed to the client before the service is provided
questions.explanation: Article 24(9) permits inducements only where they are designed to enhance the quality of the relevant service, do not impair compliance with the duty to act honestly, fairly and professionally in the client's best interests, and are clearly disclosed in advance.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an acceptable minor non-monetary benefit that an independent adviser may accept?
options: Participation in a provider's training seminar on the features of a specific financial instrument, with hospitality of a reasonable de minimis value
A cash bonus for reaching a sales target with a provider
An all-expenses-paid holiday for the adviser and family
A commission of 0.5% passed to the firm's directors
questions.explanation: Delegated Directive 2017/593 lists acceptable minor non-monetary benefits, including generic information about an instrument or service, participation in conferences or training on the benefits and features of a specific instrument, and hospitality of a reasonable de minimis value. Cash payments and lavish gifts are not minor non-monetary benefits.

questions.question: Under MiFID II product governance rules, which statement about the target market is correct?
options: Only the manufacturer has target market obligations
Only the distributor has target market obligations
The manufacturer identifies a target market of end clients, and the distributor must understand the product, identify its own target market and ensure the distribution strategy is consistent with it
Target market rules apply only to professional clients
questions.explanation: Article 16(3) and Article 24(2) impose product governance obligations on both manufacturers and distributors, which must identify target markets, regularly review products and share information.
questions.reference: Directive 2014/65/EU, Art. 16(3), Art. 24(2); Delegated Directive (EU) 2017/593, Arts. 9-10

questions.question: Which statement best describes MiFID II costs and charges disclosure to retail clients?
options: Costs need only be disclosed if the client asks
Only the product provider's charges must be disclosed; the firm's own fees are excluded
Disclosure is required once, at the start of the relationship, and never again

Aggregated information on all costs and charges, including their cumulative effect on return, must be given in good time before the service, and ex-post information must be provided at least annually where there is an ongoing relationship
questions.explanation: Article 24(4) requires ex-ante disclosure of all costs and associated charges of both the service and the instrument, aggregated and with an illustration of the cumulative effect on return. Delegated Regulation 2017/565 Article 50 requires ex-post disclosure at least annually where there is an ongoing relationship.

questions.question: When executing an order for a retail client, how is the best possible result primarily determined under MiFID II?
options: In terms of total consideration, being the price of the instrument and the costs relating to execution
By the speed of execution only
By choosing the venue that pays the firm the highest rebate
By the size of the order only
questions.explanation: Execution factors include price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size and nature. For retail clients, the best possible result is determined in terms of total consideration, being price plus all execution-related costs.

questions.question: Under MiFID II, how should a firm treat disclosure of a conflict of interest to the client?
options: As the first and only step required, replacing organisational controls

As a measure of last resort, used only where organisational and administrative arrangements are not sufficient to ensure, with reasonable confidence, that the risk of damage to client interests will be prevented
As optional where the client is a retail client
As unnecessary if the conflict is recorded internally
questions.explanation: Firms must identify, prevent or manage conflicts through effective arrangements. Disclosure is a last resort where those arrangements are insufficient, and it must be specific enough for the client to make an informed decision.

questions.question: Which of the following is a core MiFID II requirement for a firm that holds client financial instruments or client funds?
options: It may use client funds for its own working capital provided it repays them within 30 days
It may pool client assets with its own assets provided records are kept
It must make adequate arrangements to safeguard clients' ownership rights, including segregating client assets from the firm's own assets
It must transfer all client assets to the Central Bank for safekeeping
questions.explanation: Article 16(8)-(10) requires firms to safeguard client ownership rights, prevent use of client instruments for own account without express consent, and prevent use of client funds for the firm's own account. In Ireland these are supplemented by the Central Bank's Client Asset Requirements.

questions.question: MiFID II requires firms to record telephone conversations and electronic communications relating to client orders and transactions. For how long must these records generally be kept?
options: 1 year
5 years, and up to 7 years where requested by the competent authority
6 months
10 years in all cases
questions.explanation: Article 16(7) requires records of relevant communications to be provided to clients on request and kept for five years, and for up to seven years where requested by the competent authority.

questions.question: A firm provides portfolio management to a retail client. The overall value of the portfolio, as evaluated at the start of the reporting period, falls by 10%. What must the firm do?
options: Inform the client at the next quarterly statement
Sell all the assets to prevent further losses
Notify the Central Bank
Inform the client no later than the end of the business day on which the threshold is exceeded (or the next business day if it is exceeded on a non-business day), and at multiples of 10% thereafter
questions.explanation: Article 62 of Delegated Regulation 2017/565 requires portfolio managers to inform clients where the overall portfolio value depreciates by 10%, and thereafter at multiples of 10%, by the end of the business day on which the threshold is exceeded. Waiting for a periodic statement would be too late.

questions.question: Under ESMA's guidelines on knowledge and competence, a staff member who does not yet have the required qualification and experience may provide investment advice:
options: under the supervision of qualified staff, for a maximum period of four years
without any restrictions, provided the client signs a waiver
only to professional clients
under supervision for an unlimited period
questions.explanation: ESMA's guidelines require advisers to have an appropriate qualification and appropriate experience of at least six months full-time. Staff not yet meeting these may provide services under supervision, for no longer than four years.
questions.reference: ESMA Guidelines for the assessment of knowledge and competence (ESMA/2015/1886); Directive 2014/65/EU, Art. 25(1)

questions.question: An investment firm authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland under MiFID II wants to provide investment services to clients in Spain. What does the MiFID passport allow?
options: Nothing; the firm must obtain a full new authorisation in Spain
It may provide services only to Spanish professional clients
It may provide its authorised services in Spain, either cross-border or through a branch, after notifying the Central Bank, which informs the Spanish competent authority
It may provide services in Spain only if Spain and Ireland sign a bilateral agreement
questions.explanation: Articles 34 and 35 allow an authorised firm to provide services in other EEA Member States under freedom to provide services or freedom of establishment, following a notification procedure through its home competent authority.

questions.question: Which of the following are the three types of 'trading venue' under MiFID II?
options: Regulated market, systematic internaliser and broker crossing network
Regulated market, multilateral trading facility (MTF) and organised trading facility (OTF)
Stock exchange, investment bank and fund platform
Regulated market, approved publication arrangement and consolidated tape provider
questions.explanation: Trading venue means a regulated market, an MTF or an OTF. A systematic internaliser is an investment firm dealing on own account, not a trading venue, and APAs and CTPs are data reporting services.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes an organised trading facility (OTF) from a multilateral trading facility (MTF)?
options: An OTF is used only for trading shares
An OTF may only be operated by a stock exchange
An OTF does not need to be authorised
An OTF is limited to non-equity instruments such as bonds and derivatives, and its operator executes orders on a discretionary basis
questions.explanation: An OTF is a multilateral system for non-equity instruments (bonds, structured finance products, emission allowances and derivatives) in which the operator exercises discretion in executing orders. An MTF operates under non-discretionary rules and can trade equities.

questions.question: A 'systematic internaliser' under MiFID II is best described as:
options: an investment firm which, on an organised, frequent, systematic and substantial basis, deals on own account when executing client orders outside a regulated market, MTF or OTF, without operating a multilateral system
a regulated market operated by a central bank
a firm's internal compliance function for monitoring trades
an MTF that admits only retail investors
questions.explanation: A systematic internaliser executes client orders against its own book on an organised, frequent, systematic and substantial basis outside trading venues and is subject to certain transparency obligations, but is not itself a trading venue.

questions.question: Under MiFIR, investment firms that execute transactions in reportable financial instruments must report complete and accurate details of those transactions to the competent authority:
options: within 30 days
only at year end
as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the following working day
only when the competent authority requests it
questions.explanation: Article 26 MiFIR requires transaction reports as quickly as possible and no later than the close of the following working day (T+1), to support market abuse surveillance.

questions.question: Under the PRIIPs Regulation, which statement about the Key Information Document (KID) is correct?
options: It may be as long as necessary to describe the product fully
It is only required for professional investors
It may be provided after the investor has signed the contract
It is a short, standardised document of no more than three sides of A4, provided to retail investors in good time before they are bound by the contract
questions.explanation: The PRIIPs KID is a stand-alone, standardised document of at most three sides of A4 that must be provided to retail investors in good time before they are bound by any contract or offer relating to the PRIIP.

questions.question: Which statement about UCITS funds and the PRIIPs KID is correct as of 2026?
options: UCITS have never been subject to PRIIPs and still provide only the UCITS KIID
UCITS management companies have been required to provide a PRIIPs KID to retail investors since 1 January 2023, when their transitional exemption ended
UCITS must provide both a UCITS KIID and a PRIIPs KID to every retail investor
UCITS will only become subject to PRIIPs from 2030
questions.explanation: UCITS benefited from a transitional exemption from PRIIPs, which expired on 31 December 2022. From 1 January 2023 the PRIIPs KID is required for UCITS sold to retail investors, and providing a PRIIPs KID satisfies the UCITS KIID requirement.
questions.reference: Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014, Art. 32 (as amended by Regulation (EU) 2021/2259)

questions.question: A key economic rationale for regulating the sale of financial products to retail consumers is that:
options: consumers typically know far less about complex financial products than the firms that design and sell them
financial firms are generally less profitable than firms in other sectors
retail consumers usually prefer to deal with State-owned institutions
competition between financial firms always drives prices too low
questions.explanation: This is information asymmetry: the firm knows much more about the product's risks, charges and features than the consumer, who may only discover a problem years later. Regulation (disclosure, suitability, competence rules) seeks to correct this imbalance.

questions.question: The failure of one large bank causing losses and loss of confidence that spread to other banks and the wider economy is an example of:
options: information asymmetry
systemic risk
mis-selling
market abuse
questions.explanation: Systemic risk is the risk that the failure of one institution spreads through the interconnected financial system. It is a central reason for prudential regulation of banks and insurers.

questions.question: Which of the following is primarily a PRUDENTIAL regulatory concern?
options: Whether an advertisement for a savings account is clear, fair and not misleading
Whether a complaint is acknowledged within the required timeframe
Whether a bank holds sufficient capital and liquidity to absorb losses and meet its obligations
Whether an adviser provides a statement of suitability to a consumer
questions.explanation: Prudential regulation concerns the safety and soundness of firms (capital, liquidity, solvency, risk management). Advertising, complaints handling and suitability are conduct-of-business matters.

questions.question: Conduct (conduct-of-business) regulation is mainly concerned with:
options: setting interest rates for the euro area
the solvency and capital adequacy of insurance undertakings
the taxation of investment returns
how firms behave towards their customers and in the market
questions.explanation: Conduct regulation deals with how firms treat customers and behave in markets, e.g. through the Consumer Protection Code. Solvency and capital are prudential matters; interest rates are monetary policy; taxation is for Revenue.

questions.question: Deposit guarantee schemes support the aims of financial regulation mainly by:
options: maintaining depositor confidence, which reduces the risk of a run on banks
guaranteeing a minimum rate of interest on all deposits
ensuring that banks never fail
compensating depositors for poor investment advice
questions.explanation: Because depositors know their deposits are protected up to a limit, they are less likely to withdraw funds in a panic, supporting consumer confidence and financial stability. A DGS does not prevent bank failure or cover advice-related losses.

questions.question: The Central Bank Reform Act 2010 provided for:
options: the creation of the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
a single, unitary Central Bank of Ireland, bringing the former Financial Regulator's functions within the Central Bank
the establishment of the Pensions Authority
the transfer of banking supervision to the Department of Finance
questions.explanation: The 2010 Act restructured the Central Bank and Financial Services Authority of Ireland (including the Financial Regulator) into a single integrated body, the Central Bank of Ireland, responsible for both central banking and financial regulation.

questions.question: The governing body responsible for managing the affairs of the Central Bank of Ireland is:
options: the Governing Council of the European Central Bank
the Oireachtas Committee on Finance
the Central Bank Commission
the Board of the Financial Regulator
questions.explanation: Under the Central Bank Reform Act 2010, the Central Bank Commission, chaired by the Governor, is the Bank's governing body. The separate Financial Regulator board ceased to exist under the 2010 reforms.

questions.question: Under the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM), which body directly supervises euro-area banks classified as 'significant', such as Ireland's largest retail banks?
options: The European Banking Authority
The European Securities and Markets Authority
The Central Bank of Ireland acting alone
The European Central Bank
