questions.explanation: Under the SSM the ECB directly supervises significant institutions, working with national authorities such as the Central Bank of Ireland in joint supervisory teams. Less significant institutions are supervised by the national authority under ECB oversight.

questions.question: Which European Supervisory Authority covers the insurance and occupational pensions sectors?
options: EIOPA
ESMA
EBA
ESRB
questions.explanation: EIOPA is the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority. ESMA covers securities and markets, the EBA covers banking, and the ESRB is the European Systemic Risk Board (macro-prudential oversight), not one of the three ESAs.

questions.question: The Minimum Competency Code 2017 was revised to reflect guidelines on the knowledge and competence of staff giving investment advice or information under MiFID II. Which body issued those guidelines?
options: EIOPA
ESMA
The EBA
The ECB
questions.explanation: The ESMA Guidelines for the assessment of knowledge and competence under MiFID II were implemented in Ireland through the MCC 2017 and the Minimum Competency Regulations 2017.
questions.reference: Central Bank MCC 2017 / MCR 2017 Q&A, Q2.2

questions.question: The main role of the European Banking Authority (EBA) is to:
options: directly supervise every bank in the European Union
set the interest rates for the euro area
develop a single rulebook and promote consistent supervision of banks across the EU
operate the deposit guarantee schemes of each Member State
questions.explanation: The EBA contributes to a single rulebook (technical standards and guidelines) and supervisory convergence. Direct supervision of significant euro-area banks is the ECB's role under the SSM; interest rates are set by the ECB; DGSs are national schemes.
questions.reference: European System of Financial Supervision - EBA

questions.question: Under the Central Bank Reform Act 2010, a person may be appointed to a pre-approval controlled function (PCF) only when:
options: the firm has notified the Central Bank within 30 days after the appointment
the person has completed the QFA
the firm's board has approved the appointment
the Central Bank has approved the appointment in advance
questions.explanation: PCF roles (e.g. directors, CEO, heads of key functions) require the Central Bank's prior written approval before the person takes up the role. Board approval and qualifications alone are not sufficient.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a controlled function (CF) and a pre-approval controlled function (PCF)?
options: The Central Bank must approve a PCF holder before appointment; for a CF, the firm itself must be satisfied that the person meets the Fitness and Probity Standards
The Fitness and Probity Standards apply only to PCF holders, not CF holders
CF holders must be approved by the Central Bank, while PCF holders are approved by the firm
CF roles exist only in credit unions
questions.explanation: Both CF and PCF holders must meet the Fitness and Probity Standards and a firm must not permit anyone to perform a CF unless satisfied on reasonable grounds that they comply. Only PCF appointments need the Central Bank's prior approval.

questions.question: After an investigation under Part 3 of the Central Bank Reform Act 2010, the Central Bank concludes that an individual is not fit and proper. Which instrument can it use to bar that person from performing a controlled function?
options: A suspension notice
A prohibition notice
A section 48 direction
A revocation order
questions.explanation: A prohibition notice (s.43) prohibits a person from carrying out a controlled function. A suspension notice (s.26) is a temporary measure while an investigation into fitness and probity is ongoing.
questions.reference: Central Bank Reform Act 2010, ss.26 and 43

questions.question: The Central Bank's Fitness and Probity Standards require a person performing a controlled function to be:
options: resident in Ireland and a shareholder of the firm
a holder of a university degree in finance
competent and capable; honest, ethical and acting with integrity; and financially sound
approved in advance by the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
questions.explanation: The Standards (issued under s.50 of the 2010 Act) cover three elements: competence and capability, honesty/ethics/integrity, and financial soundness. There is no residency, shareholding or degree requirement.
questions.reference: Central Bank Fitness and Probity Standards (s.50, Central Bank Reform Act 2010)

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the four pillars of the Individual Accountability Framework (IAF)?
options: The Minimum Competency Code
The Deposit Guarantee Scheme
The Consumer Protection Code
The Senior Executive Accountability Regime (SEAR)
questions.explanation: The IAF's four pillars are SEAR, the Conduct Standards, enhancements to the Fitness and Probity regime, and enhancements to the Administrative Sanctions Procedure.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023; Central Bank IAF guidance

questions.question: To whom do the Common Conduct Standards under the IAF apply?
options: All individuals performing controlled function roles (both CF and PCF) in regulated firms
Only PCF holders in firms within the scope of SEAR
Only independent non-executive directors
Only customer-facing staff who hold a recognised qualification
questions.explanation: The Common Conduct Standards apply to everyone in a CF role, including PCFs, in all regulated firms - not just SEAR firms. Firms must make CF holders aware of them.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023; Conduct Standards Regulations

questions.question: The Additional Conduct Standards under the IAF apply to:
options: all employees of a regulated firm
PCF holders and those in CF-1 roles who can exercise significant influence on the conduct of the firm's affairs
only executive directors of banks
only staff providing MiFID investment advice
questions.explanation: The Additional Conduct Standards (e.g. ensuring the business is controlled effectively) apply to PCF holders and CF-1 role holders, whether or not the firm is within SEAR.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023; Central Bank IAF guidance

questions.question: Which of the following is a COMMON Conduct Standard that applies to every person in a controlled function?
options: Ensure that the business of the firm is controlled effectively
Ensure that any delegation of tasks is to an appropriate person with effective oversight
Act in the best interests of customers and treat them fairly and professionally
Ensure that the firm's business complies with financial services legislation
questions.explanation: Acting in customers' best interests and treating them fairly and professionally is a Common Conduct Standard (with honesty and integrity, due skill care and diligence, co-operation with the Central Bank and market conduct). The other options are Additional Conduct Standards for senior roles.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023; Conduct Standards

questions.question: From what date did the IAF Conduct Standards for individuals begin to apply?
options: 1 January 2023
1 July 2024
24 March 2026
29 December 2023
questions.explanation: The remaining parts of the IAF Act were commenced and the Conduct Standards applied from 29 December 2023. SEAR began applying to executive PCF roles in in-scope firms from 1 July 2024; the revised Consumer Protection Code applied from 24 March 2026.
questions.reference: Central Bank IAF webpage - key dates

questions.question: Under SEAR, an in-scope firm must document where responsibility lies by:
options: preparing a Statement of Responsibilities for each relevant senior individual and maintaining a Management Responsibilities Map
obtaining a personal guarantee from each director
having every customer contract signed by a PCF holder
publishing the remuneration of every controlled function holder
questions.explanation: SEAR requires in-scope firms to allocate prescribed responsibilities, set out each senior executive's responsibilities in a Statement of Responsibilities, and maintain a Management Responsibilities Map of governance arrangements.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023, SEAR

questions.question: The 'duty of responsibility' under SEAR requires a senior executive to:
options: guarantee that the firm never breaches any regulation, regardless of the steps taken
take reasonable steps to avoid the firm committing, or continuing to commit, a prescribed contravention in the areas for which they are responsible
personally approve every product sold by the firm
personally compensate customers for any loss caused by the firm
questions.explanation: The duty of responsibility is a 'reasonable steps' duty linked to the executive's own areas of responsibility; it is not strict liability. Acting reasonably in all the circumstances is the key defence.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023, SEAR

questions.question: Under the IAF enhancements to the Fitness and Probity regime, regulated firms must:
options: obtain Central Bank pre-approval for every new employee
require every CF holder to pass an annual Central Bank examination
certify that individuals in CF and PCF roles meet the Fitness and Probity Standards
publish the F&P assessments of their staff on their website
questions.explanation: Firms must proactively certify that people in CF and PCF roles meet the Fitness and Probity Standards (the Certification Regulations applied from 8 January 2024). Pre-approval is still required only for PCFs.
questions.reference: Central Bank IAF guidance - F&P enhancements

questions.question: What significant change to the Administrative Sanctions Procedure did the Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023 introduce?
options: The ASP was abolished and replaced by criminal prosecution only
Sanctions may now be imposed only on firms, not individuals
All ASP cases must now be decided by the High Court
The Central Bank can pursue individuals directly for breaches of their own obligations, e.g. the Conduct Standards, without first proving a breach by the firm
questions.explanation: Previously, action against individuals depended on showing they participated in a firm's contravention. The 2023 Act allows the Central Bank to take ASP action directly against individuals for breaching their own obligations.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023; Central Bank Act 1942, Part IIIC

questions.question: The Central Bank's Administrative Sanctions Procedure (ASP) is set out in:
options: Part IIIC of the Central Bank Act 1942 (as amended)
Part 3 of the Central Bank Reform Act 2010
the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
the Consumer Protection Code
questions.explanation: The ASP is provided for in Part IIIC of the Central Bank Act 1942, as amended (most recently by the IAF Act 2023). Part 3 of the 2010 Act is the Fitness and Probity regime.

questions.question: Under the ASP, the maximum monetary penalty that may be imposed on a regulated firm is:
options: €1 million
the greater of €10 million or 10% of the firm's turnover
the greater of €5 million or 5% of the firm's profits
questions.explanation: The maximum fine for a firm is the greater of €10 million or 10% of turnover (as of 2026). The maximum for an individual is €1 million.

questions.question: The main role of the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO) is to:
options: authorise financial service providers to operate in Ireland
prosecute firms that operate without authorisation
independently investigate and decide complaints from consumers against financial service and pension providers
pay compensation to depositors when a bank fails
questions.explanation: The FSPO is an independent, free dispute-resolution service for complaints against financial service providers and pension providers. Authorisation and enforcement are Central Bank functions; deposit compensation is paid by the DGS.
questions.reference: Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman Act 2017

questions.question: In a complaint that does not relate to an annuity, what is the maximum compensation the FSPO can direct a financial service provider to pay?
questions.explanation: The FSPO can direct compensation of up to €500,000 (a lower limit applies to annuity complaints), as of 2026. It can also direct the provider to rectify the conduct complained of.

questions.question: A legally binding decision of the FSPO can be challenged by either party by:
options: an appeal to the High Court
an appeal to the Central Bank
an appeal to the Circuit Court
a request to the CCPC to review it
questions.explanation: FSPO decisions are binding on both parties, subject only to a statutory appeal to the High Court, normally within 35 calendar days of the decision.
questions.reference: FSPO Act 2017 (appeals to the High Court)

questions.question: Which body has a statutory role in providing consumers with information and education about financial products, for example through money comparison tools?
options: Revenue
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC)
The Pensions Authority
The European Central Bank
questions.explanation: The CCPC promotes consumer welfare and competition and has a financial information and education role for consumers, including comparison tools. It does not authorise or supervise financial firms - that is the Central Bank.
questions.reference: Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2014; ccpc.ie

questions.question: Under the Irish Deposit Guarantee Scheme, eligible deposits are protected up to:
options: €20,000 per person per institution
€50,000 per account
€100,000 per person per institution
€100,000 per account, with no per-person limit
questions.explanation: The DGS protects up to €100,000 per person per institution (as of 2026), regardless of how many accounts the person holds with that institution.
questions.reference: Central Bank Consumer Hub - compensation schemes; Deposit Guarantee Scheme

questions.question: Mary has savings in a credit union authorised by the Central Bank of Ireland. If the credit union fails, her savings are:
options: not protected, because credit unions are outside all compensation schemes
protected by the Investor Compensation Scheme at 90% up to €20,000
protected by the Insurance Compensation Fund
protected by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme up to €100,000
questions.explanation: Savings in banks, building societies and credit unions authorised by the Central Bank are covered by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme up to €100,000 per person per institution.
questions.reference: Central Bank Consumer Hub - compensation schemes

questions.question: Seán's authorised investment firm is placed into liquidation and cannot return €30,000 of client money owed to him. What is the maximum he can receive from the Investor Compensation Scheme?
questions.explanation: The ICS pays 90% of the eligible net loss subject to a maximum of €20,000 (as of 2026). 90% of €30,000 is €27,000, so the €20,000 cap applies.
questions.reference: Investor Compensation Act 1998; Central Bank Consumer Hub

questions.question: In which situation may the Investor Compensation Scheme pay compensation?
options: An investment fund falls in value because of stock market conditions
An authorised investment firm cannot return clients' money or investment instruments and has been placed in liquidation or found unable to meet its obligations
A solvent intermediary gave unsuitable advice and the client wants redress
A client regrets an investment decision made on an execution-only basis
questions.explanation: The ICS is triggered when an authorised firm cannot return client money or instruments (liquidation or a Central Bank determination). It does not cover market losses or bad advice; a complaint about advice from a solvent firm would go to the firm and then the FSPO.
questions.reference: Investor Compensation Act 1998; Central Bank Consumer Hub

questions.question: Ciara has a valid €20,000 household insurance claim against an Irish-authorised non-life insurer that has gone into liquidation. Under the Insurance Compensation Fund, the most she can expect is:
options: nothing, because household insurance is excluded
questions.explanation: The ICF pays 65% of the claim or €825,000, whichever is lower (as of 2026), for non-life policies such as home and motor. 65% of €20,000 is €13,000. Life and health insurance are excluded.
questions.reference: Insurance Act 1964 (as amended); Central Bank Consumer Hub

questions.question: Which body regulates occupational pension schemes and their trustees in Ireland?
options: The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
Revenue
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
The Pensions Authority
questions.explanation: The Pensions Authority regulates occupational pension schemes, trustees and PRSA products under the Pensions Act 1990. The FSPO resolves complaints; Revenue grants tax approval.

questions.question: Which of the following is a role of Revenue in relation to financial services?
options: Approving pension arrangements for tax relief purposes and collecting taxes such as DIRT and exit tax
Authorising insurance intermediaries
Adjudicating consumer complaints against banks
Supervising the solvency of credit unions
questions.explanation: Revenue deals with the tax treatment of financial products, including approving pension arrangements for tax relief and collecting taxes like DIRT and exit tax. Authorisation and supervision are Central Bank functions; complaints go to the FSPO.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of the Central Bank of Ireland?
options: Setting the rates of income tax
Protecting consumers of financial services through regulation and supervision
Making binding decisions on individual consumer complaints against firms
Independently setting interest rates for Ireland
questions.explanation: Consumer protection is one of the Central Bank's core functions, alongside financial stability and prudential supervision. Individual complaints are decided by the FSPO, and euro-area interest rates are set by the ECB Governing Council.
questions.reference: Central Bank Act 1942 (as amended by the Central Bank Reform Act 2010)

questions.question: The Central Bank (Supervision and Enforcement) Act 2013 (Section 48) (Consumer Protection) Regulations 2025 - part of the revised Consumer Protection Code - were made using the Central Bank's power under:
options: section 9 of the Central Bank Act 1971
section 50 of the Central Bank Reform Act 2010
section 48 of the Central Bank (Supervision and Enforcement) Act 2013
the Investment Intermediaries Act 1995
questions.explanation: Section 48 of the 2013 Act allows the Central Bank to make regulations for the proper and effective regulation of financial service providers, including consumer protection. Section 50 of the 2010 Act is used for Fitness and Probity Standards and the MCC.
questions.reference: Central Bank (Supervision and Enforcement) Act 2013, s.48; S.I. No. 81 of 2025

questions.question: The Central Bank Reform Act 2010 (Section 17A) (Standards for Business) Regulations 2025, which apply from 24 March 2026, require a regulated entity at all times to:
options: maximise the investment returns of its customers
guarantee that no customer suffers a financial loss
obtain Central Bank approval before launching any new product
secure its customers' interests, act honestly and with integrity, and act with due skill, care and diligence
questions.explanation: The Standards for Business, made under s.17A of the 2010 Act (inserted by the IAF Act 2023), require firms to secure customers' interests, act honestly and with integrity, and act with due skill, care and diligence, among other standards.
questions.reference: S.I. No. 80 of 2025, Standards for Business Regulations
